title: 'Hercules' star Kevin Sorbo says California can keep its taxes, traffic and 'negativity': 'I'm done'
summary: "Elijah Peel" actor Kevin Sorbo says California can keep its taxes, traffic, and "negativity" after moving to Florida nearly seven years ago for his family and career.
story: ‘Elijah Peel’ actor tells Fox News Digital how Florida delivered ‘acceptance,’ new connections and filmmaking opportunities after he left California.
Kevin Sorbo has officially closed the door on California.
Nearly seven years after leaving the Golden State for Florida, the "Hercules" star says he has no interest in going back — and he's got three reasons why: "Taxes, traffic and negativity."

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Sorbo, who stars in the faith-based movie "Elijah Peel," said his move to Florida has given him something he felt was increasingly difficult to find in California — "acceptance."
KEVIN SORBO BLASTS HOLLYWOOD 'BLACKLISTING' OF CONSERVATIVES AS 'SEVENTH GRADE MEAN GIRLS' CULTURE
Kevin Sorbo has blasted California over its taxes, traffic and what he described as widespread "negativity." (AP Images)
The actor said he still misses Westlake Village, Thousand Oaks, his golf course, his old house and California's famously mild weather. But the trade-off, he said, isn't worth it.

"I mean, here in Florida, yeah, we get five months of pretty high humidity. It's pretty hot, but the winters here are really quite amazing," Sorbo said. "But yeah, there are things I miss, but they can keep their taxes, they can keep their traffic, and they can keep their negativity, I'm done."
WATCH: KEVIN SORBO REJECTS CALIFORNIA RETURN: ‘THEY CAN KEEP THEIR NEGATIVITY, I’M DONE’
For Sorbo, the California exit wasn't simply a change of scenery.
The actor said the independent film community has embraced him, with filmmakers and creators from across the country reaching out through his production company, Sorbo Studios.
A scene from "Elijah Peel," a film inspired by a true story about a rock star whose recovery leads to an unexpected bond with a young girl. (EKKL Entertainment)
KELSEY GRAMMER SUSPECTS HE 'MAY HAVE' LOST HOLLYWOOD ROLES DUE TO CONSERVATIVE VIEWS
"The people I've met here, the contacts I've met, it's been incredible," he said.
Sorbo took aim at the entertainment industry, which he believes has punished people for holding certain political or religious views.
WATCH: ACTOR KEVIN SORBO TOUTS ‘ELIJAH PEEL’ FOR WHAT HOLLYWOOD ABANDONED
The actor, who has been outspoken about his faith and politics, compared Hollywood's treatment of conservatives and Christians to childish antics seen in schools, not a multimillion-dollar industry.

"That's why I find a lot of things in Hollywood, with their blacklisting people that have conservative or Christian viewpoints, I find it like they're seventh grade mean girls," Sorbo told Fox News Digital.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Sorbo is best known for his roles as Hercules in "Hercules: The Legendary Journeys" and Captain Dylan Hunt in "Andromeda." (Maureen Donaldson / Getty Images)
"It's just ridiculous and childish to me. We all have different opinions. There's nothing wrong with that."
Sorbo has previously described himself as someone who has been "canceled" for his views. But he said the experience hasn't convinced him to stay quiet.
WATCH: ACTOR KEVIN SORBO SAYS ‘DEMONIC STUFF’ IS HAPPENING IN HOLLYWOOD
Instead, he's challenging other conservatives in Hollywood to stop hiding.
"It's the conservatives that are in the closet now because they saw me get canceled," Sorbo said. "But I'm still working."
Sorbo's comments came as his latest film, "Elijah Peel," hit theaters — a faith-based drama inspired by a true story.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

The movie follows a rock star whose meteoric career and struggle with addiction spiral after a near-fatal heart attack. A young girl's faith ultimately forces him to confront the life he's been living.
Sorbo portrays the musician's longtime talent manager.
Willie and Korie Robertson of "Duck Dynasty" serve as executive producers, adding another prominent Christian entertainment connection to the project.
And Sorbo believes movies like "Elijah Peel" demonstrate that faith-based filmmakers no longer need Hollywood's blessing.
The movie "Elijah Peel" is inspired by a true story and from executive producers Willie and Korie Robertson. (EKKL Entertainment)
The audience is already there, he argued.
"There’s 80 million homes in America that want the kind of movies that I've been fortunate to be part of — that is going to keep on growing," Sorbo said.
Away from the cameras, Sorbo said his marriage and family have remained his top priorities through career changes, health scares and the ups and downs of life in Hollywood.
Sorbo also opened up about the nearly three decades he has spent married to his wife, Sam, crediting humor, compromise and family for keeping their relationship strong.

Kevin Sorbo and his wife, actress Sam Sorbo, have been married for nearly three decades and share three children. (Michael Tran/Getty Images)
When Fox News Digital asked about the foundation of his marriage, Sorbo laughed and replied, "Oh, that's easy. I just say yes to her all the time. I just agree with everything she tells me."
He added, "We have our disagreements, but we've always gone through those with no problem. And we've overcome those things."
Family remains the priority, Sorbo emphasized.
"My boys are now 24 and 22, my daughter's 20."

The Sorbos are also outspoken advocates for homeschooling, with Sorbo's wife traveling around the country to share what they see as the benefits of educating children outside the traditional public-school system.

"We never experienced terrible teens with my kids. We just didn't. They're hardworking, they're awesome, and they're just good people," Sorbo said.

title: Dolly Parton once performed for Queen Elizabeth II and was 'scared to death' about her curtsy
summary: Dolly Parton recalled being "scared to death" about curtsying when she performed for Queen Elizabeth II during the Queen's Silver Jubilee in 1977.
story: Britain's Band of the Coldstream Guards played Dolly Parton’s iconic "9 to 5" outside Buckingham Palace in a royal tribute to the county music star following her death Tuesday.
Country royalty met actual royalty in 1977 when Dolly Parton performed for Queen Elizabeth II.
And despite her success, the "Jolene" superstar’s boots were shaking a bit when she had her audience with the monarch.

"I remember as a child being fascinated with the kings and queens and all their flamboyant clothes, people living in another world with riches and crowns and jewelry and all that," Parton told Business Insider after the queen’s death. "But when I actually got to meet her, she was very sweet."
DOLLY PARTON'S LIFE IN HER OWN WORDS: FROM SMOKY MOUNTAINS POVERTY TO COUNTRY MUSIC IMMORTALITY
Dolly Parton performed for Queen Elizabeth II at her Silver Jubilee in 1977. (Keystone/Getty Images; Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

"That's just something she had to do, and if somebody made a mistake, it was OK."

British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard said Parton’s death this week is "comparable to losing our late Great Queen Elizabeth II... Two strong and resilient female figures."

title: Jimi Hendrix’s final words to roadie revealed after violent Hells Angels clash
summary: Eric Barrett recalls Jimi Hendrix's final concert at the Isle of Fehmarn, where Hells Angels violence forced a harrowing escape before his death.
story: Carlos Santana recalls the moment he impressed Jimi Hendrix
It was supposed to be another stop on the road for Jimi Hendrix — but a festival marred by violence and chaos would become the rock legend's final official concert performance.

Eric Barrett, who was Hendrix's roadie and confidant from 1968 to 1970, has written a memoir, "Experienced: On the Road with Jimi Hendrix and Beyond." Barrett went on to spend nearly five decades working behind the scenes with other iconic artists, including Madonna, David Bowie and Aerosmith.

"We were playing on the Isle of Fehmarn, and the Hells Angels had taken over," Barrett recalled to Fox News Digital. "There was no control. It was a scary place to be. We had two cars there waiting to get us off the island and go back to London. But the Hells Angels didn't want us to get off the island. They wanted the boys to stay and party. And then it got violent."
PAUL MCCARTNEY REVEALS HOW A 'HAPPY' TEEN HITCHHIKING TRIP WITH GEORGE HARRISON DELIVERED A SHOCK
Jimi Hendrix is the subject of a new book by his roadie and tour manager, Eric Barrett, titled, "Experienced: On the Road with Jimi Hendrix and Beyond." (David Redfern/Redferns)

According to Barrett's book, hundreds of Hells Angels descended on the island and took over the venue. He wrote that many fans who had been camping out were "beaten and robbed" as festival security was chased off. Hendrix, he said, took one look at the mayhem and retreated to his room "alone, sober." The outlaw motorcycle club had taken over.

The next day, Hendrix took the stage and was met with boos. He told the hostile audience, "I don't give a f--- if you boo, as long as you boo in key, you mothers," before chuckling. When he was done, Hendrix told the audience, "Thank you, goodbye. Peace!"
"Experienced: On the Road with Jimi Hendrix and Beyond" by Eric Barrett is out now. (Diversion Books)
Barrett ushered Hendrix and the band off the stage toward the waiting cars. Barrett was eager to get out. But then the bikers surrounded them.
WATCH: CARLOS SANTANA RECALLS THE MOMENT HE IMPRESSED JIMI HENDRIX: ‘I’LL TAKE IT’

"I saw a Hells Angel about to hit [tour manager] Gerry Stickells over the head with this baton," said Barrett. "I put my arm up to take the blow. I nearly passed out from the pain, but imagine if it had landed on Gerry's skull? We managed to get inside the car. Jimi kept looking at me because he saw me take the blow. He just said to me, 'Are you OK, Eric? Are you OK?' He kept asking me if I was OK. That's just the kind of man he was. And... that was the last thing he ever said to me."
Eric Barrett was Jimi Hendrix's roadie from 1968 to 1970. (Courtesy of Eric Barrett)
On Sept. 18, 1970, paramedics arrived at Monika Dannemann's apartment at the Samarkand Hotel in London and found Hendrix unresponsive. He was 27.
Stickells broke the news to Barrett.
An exterior view of the former Samarkand Hotel in London, where Jimi Hendrix died in 1970. (Future Publishing via Getty Images)

"I couldn't believe it," said Barrett. "I remember walking around London in a fog. It was a stupid, tragic accident. He took too many of [girlfriend] Monika Dannemann's sleeping pills. She supposedly had these incredibly powerful German tranquilizers. And she said he took nine of them. She couldn't wake him. She called Eric Burdon of The Animals, who was a good friend of Jimi's. He screamed at her, 'Call the f-----g ambulance!'"
From left: Friends Jimi Hendrix, Eric Burdon and Noel Redding. (Sygma via Getty Images)
"What I'm being told was the ambulance guys ... laid him on his back, and he threw up," said Barrett. "He asphyxiated. That was the accident. The pills were the accident. Tragedy was him dying."
Jimi Hendrix performs at the Isle of Wight festival on August 29, 1970. (Jean-Pierre Leloir)

In the book, Barrett wrote, "The paramedics arrived but couldn't revive Jimi. They carried him out on a stretcher to the ambulance, assuring Monika that he was going to be all right. Either lying in bed on his back or on the way to the hospital, Jimi threw up on himself. The post-mortem concluded that Jimi had died of asphyxia while intoxicated with barbiturates."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Monika Dannemann is seen here outside the building where Jimi Hendrix died. (Brian Aris/Mirrorpix)

"... I flashed back to the time I took too much Mandrax, and my girlfriend couldn't wake me up," he wrote. "It was easily done and could've happened to any of us in Jimi's group of friends. That it happened to Jimi himself was heartbreaking. But I've never heard anything to make me think Jimi's death was anything other than what it appeared."
Rock guitarist Jimi Hendrix is seen here with Eric Barrett at Heathrow Airport after flying in from New York on his way to the Isle of Wight pop festival. (PA Images via Getty Images)

Barrett firmly rejected the rumors and conspiracy theories that have surrounded Hendrix's death for decades. Among them was an allegation by former roadie James "Tappy" Wright, who wrote in his 2009 memoir, "Rock Roadie," that Hendrix’s manager, Mike Jeffery, confessed to killing Hendrix, The Guardian reported.
Barrett strongly disputes Wright's account and rejects any suggestion that Hendrix was murdered.
Manager Michael "Mike" Jeffery is seen outside Marylebone Register Office in June 1965. (Mirrorpix via Getty Images)

"I don't believe for a second that Mike Jeffery was the cause of Jimi's death," he said. "I just don't believe it. The circumstances don't add up. And I was told by so many people that Tappy only wrote that to try and sell books. But I've never believed it. I will never believe it. I was there, and right now I'm probably the last man standing. All the lads are passing. So no, I wouldn't believe that for a second."
Jeffery died in a plane crash near Nantes, France, in 1973.
Jimi Hendrix and Eric Barrett are seen here at the Hollywood Bowl. (Chris Boyd)

Dannemann died in an apparent suicide in 1996, two days after she was found guilty of contempt of court in a long-running legal dispute with Kathy Etchingham, another former girlfriend of Hendrix's. She was 50.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
German painter and former figure skater Monika Dannemann holds a palette and brush as she works on one of her paintings in London, England, circa 1970. (Getty Images)
Barrett said that shortly after Hendrix's death, he lied to reporters about Hendrix's drug use.

"I was, what, 24 when he passed?" said Barrett. "I didn't want to besmirch his memory. So I lied. I just wanted people to see him in a good light. But I came to realize as I got older that I didn't have to lie. Yes, he took drugs. Did he take heroin? I've never seen heroin anywhere near him. I've worked on many backstages for almost 50 years. I know it's a drug that has killed a lot of musicians. But I don't believe Jimi was taking it. He smoked pot. He took a lot of LSD. He took pills. But I don't believe he was into heroin."
Eric Barrett watches over Jimi Hendrix as he performs in Zurich. (Johannes Bruell courtesy of the Marcel Aeby Collection)

Looking back, Barrett described Hendrix as "a wild man" on stage. The musician was famous for playing the guitar behind his head and with his teeth. He would also smash guitars and amps during encores and, on occasion, set his guitar on fire. But when the shows were over and audiences had long since left, Hendrix was a "quiet, mild-mannered, polite young man."
Rock guitarist Jimi Hendrix plays his Fender Stratocaster with his teeth at his last concert on Sept. 6, 1970, on the Isle of Fehmarn, Germany. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)

"He talked to everyone," he said. "He was very charming. And he was shy. People were in awe of Jimi. And when he had his guitar around his neck, over his shoulder, he was comfortable. That was his crutch. But I also remember Paul McCartney walking towards him, and he's gasping, 'It's Paul McCartney!' He was just a shy man who didn't know how to take the accolades of his talent."
"At the Shokan House before Woodstock, trying to teach a very stoned Jimi to ride," said Eric Barrett. (Willis Hogan Jr./David Pearcy Collection)

"I have so many memories of that wonderful man," Barrett continued. "I remember we were all staying in Benedict Canyon and it was my birthday. We were all hanging out by the pool, and Jimi came out in no shirt, just velvet pants. He goes, 'Eric, Eric!' I responded, 'Hey Jimi, what do you need?' He smiled and went, 'Happy birthday, man. Here's some money. Go and buy yourself something you really want.' He gave me $500, which was a huge amount back then."
Jimi Hendrix and Eric Barrett at Benedict Canyon. (Courtesy of Eric Barrett)

"I went to North Beach Leathers, a place I'd seen Jimi had bought some clothes from. I bought myself this long leather coat, spent all my money on it. It was the best gift I ever bought. When I came back, he loved it. He went, 'Wow, that's a coat! I wish I had seen that before you.'"

Rock guitarist Jimi Hendrix performs onstage with his Fender Stratocaster electric guitar at his last concert on Sept. 6, 1970, on the Isle of Fehmarn, Germany. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
Barrett said he carries "beautiful memories" of Hendrix. One in particular has never left him.

"With Jimi at TTG Studios in Los Angeles," said Eric Barrett. "He replaced my tambourine with a beer." (Michael Ochs)

"I was on a plane with him after a show," he said. "Jimi looked at me and said, 'Eric, what do you think, will they remember me?' I was flabbergasted. I went, 'Will they remember you? You're huge over here.' But he was so insecure. 'Are you sure, Eric? What if the kids don't come?' I just told him, 'When it comes to success, you have nothing to worry about.' That was Jimi, a gift to the Earth from the Lord. And I miss him."

title: Country duo Dan + Shay nearly broke up at height of success when their communication faltered
summary: Dan + Shay reveal the late-night conversation at Dan Smyers' home that saved their partnership after a 2021 communication breakdown nearly ended it all.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Country music duo Dan + Shay revealed they almost went their separate ways at the height of their success.

The duo, composed of Dan Smyers, 39, and Shay Mooney, 34, admitted while on the "Artist Friendly" podcast recently that, at the pinnacle of their success, "there was unhealthy dynamics between both of us 'cause we process things a lot differently."
Mooney explained that their biggest issue was that there "was just a communication stop," and they eventually "got to this point" where it was "just getting really tough."

"We had that moment in 2021, and it was kind of like, all right, do we ride off into the sunset and celebrate our accomplishments or do, like, we have some maybe really hard conversations with each other and fix this?" Mooney said.
The country music duo said they almost broke up at the height of their success. (David Becker/Getty Images)
COUNTRY STAR STEPS AWAY FROM MUSIC TO FOCUS ON HIMSELF AFTER FAME TOOK A TOLL

After host Joel Madden pressed the duo for more details, Smyers explained that, after they landed the opening slot for Kenny Chesney's tour, they were excited but didn't know if they could do it since their relationship was in a bad place.
They ultimately decided, "We have to figure this out," even if it meant that they "call it a day and go out on this Kenny tour as our farewell tour," Smyers said.
The two decided to meet at Smyers' home to have a conversation, with Smyers calling that meeting "the most pivotal critical moment in our entire career."
"We're either going to say peace out to this thing or we're going to figure this out and get it right," Mooney said.
Smyers added, "He ended up staying at the house till like 3, 4 in the morning and just hashing."
The duo had a meeting to discuss how they were going to move forward. (Sebron Snyder/Penske Media via Getty Images)

Mooney later explained that he felt as if Smyers wasn't enjoying himself during the shows, noting that he felt like he didn't "know how to make you enjoy these things" and that he just wanted his friend to be happy.

He was later able to understand that Smyers is particular about "those details that people don't see" and would get upset when things malfunction during shows, for instance, if "the video wall was out," whereas that isn't as big of an issue for Mooney.

"When we finally were like, 'Hey, you're not good at enjoying these things sometimes. I enjoy everything even when it's bad,'" Mooney said. "So, if we can meet somewhere in the middle, we can make this beautiful thing. Which is what happened in the beginning."

In the end, they chose to remain together as a duo after they both apologized for their part in the breakdown of their relationship. Smyers said they also established a new rule by which they let each other know when something is bothering them "rather than letting these things build up and boil and then it just explodes."

title: Comedian Leanne Morgan calls out Hollywood for living in a 'bubble' and misjudging what audiences want to see
summary: Comedian Leanne Morgan says Hollywood lives in a "bubble" and reveals she pushed back on a cursing scene while filming with Reese Witherspoon.
story: Candace Cameron Bure, known for ‘Full House,’ shares her deeply personal faith journey, revealing she embraced Christianity at age 12.
Comedian Leanne Morgan is calling out Hollywood for living in a "bubble."

During a recent appearance on "The Women of Joy Show" podcast, the 60-year-old actress discussed the idea that Christian women don't consume media with host Maegan Waldrep Schwindling, saying they want "quality" content but without "women in their panties shooting bows and arrows and all the things like it."

"Honest to goodness, I think in the secular world, I think people, no, I think a lot of people don't want to see all that," she said. "I think a lot of people don't want to see all that, and I think they're in a bubble out there. And they think people want to see that, but they're not in the middle of the United States."

She gave an example from when she was filming a movie with Reese Witherspoon and Will Ferrell in which she played a Southern mother of four who, in the script, was meant to curse in front of her children.
Morgan called out Hollywood for being in a "bubble." (Dominik Bindl/Getty Images)
FORMER DISNEY STAR DAVID HENRIE REJECTED 'SECULAR' HOLLYWOOD LIFESTYLE AFTER LIFE-CHANGING MONASTERY VISIT

Morgan recalled telling the director that a Southern mother of four "wouldn't talk like that in front of these children." In that case, the director, Nick Stoller, told her, "You know better than I do, Leanne, and you do what you think is best."

"So I think they think in their minds, 'Oh, everybody's talking like this, everybody wants this,' but I don't think the majority of people do," she said. "Or not in the South, especially when you're portraying Southern characters. Or anywhere really."
She also explained that, growing up, no one in her family used swear words and while "it's OK if somebody else wants to use it," she doesn't care to use them herself.
The comedian is now starring in the Netflix show, "Leanne," in which she portrays a Southern mother in her 50s who is rebuilding her life after her husband left her for a younger woman.

She admitted that she felt a "darkness" when she moved to Los Angeles to film her show and that her "boys sent me a Bible study" she could do on her own. Her friend found her a church to attend.

In addition to making sure Southern Christians were not stereotyped on her show, she also felt the pressure to make sure the show was a success, saying she was reminded all the time how much it cost to make the show and how many people were relying on it.
"I've prayed more than I've ever prayed in my life," Morgan said.

"I really relied on my faith and would pray, 'God get me through this,'" she added. "I just had to rely on the Lord and know that he had me there. There's a reason for me to be there. But I could feel that every day. Every day."

title: 7 new dementia risk factors revealed — including one millions struggle with
summary: The World Health Organization has added seven new dementia risk factors, including stroke, sleep apnea, HIV and air pollution, to its updated guidelines.
story: Psychiatrist Daniel Amen discusses updated global recommendations for reducing cognitive decline, highlighting hormones, cardiovascular health, restorative rest, sensory loss, social connection and other factors tied to healthy aging.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has released a major update to its guidelines on reducing the risk of cognitive decline and dementia.
The second edition of the original 2019 report was updated to "reflect the latest evidence and advances in dementia risk reduction."
The following seven additional health conditions and exposures were added to the list.
LEARNING ANOTHER LANGUAGE MAY KEEP YOUR BRAIN YOUNGER, STUDY SUGGESTS
Stroke
Traumatic brain injury
Vision impairment
Sleep problems
HIV
Air pollution
Menopausal hormone therapy
The WHO's updated guidelines "reflect the latest evidence and advances in dementia risk reduction." (iStock)
These new risk factors joined the previously existing 12, which are listed below.
Cognitive activity
Social activity
Physical inactivity
Harmful alcohol use
Tobacco use
Unhealthy diet/nutrition
Obesity
Diabetes
Hypertension
Dyslipidemia (abnormal amount of lipids (fats) or lipoproteins in the blood)
Hearing loss
Depression
WARDING OFF ALZHEIMER'S MIGHT MEAN MAKING THESE 11 LIFESTYLE CHANGES, EXPERT SAYS
Dr. Daniel Amen, physician and founder of Amen Clinics in California, has his own formula for reducing Alzheimer’s risk factors, following an acronym called BRIGHT MINDS.

This stands for blood flow, retirement and aging, inflammation, genetics, head trauma, toxins, mental health, immunity and infections, neurohormones, diabesity (co-occurrence of obesity and type 2 diabetes) and sleep. The WHO’s updated guidelines offer similar advice.
Menopausal hormone therapy is primarily used to treat symptoms of menopause. (iStock)
Amen spoke with Fox News Digital about the new additions to the WHO's list of risk factors.
Menopausal hormone therapy (MHT)

The WHO does not recommend menopausal hormone therapy specifically to prevent dementia in postmenopausal women 65 and older. For younger women, it says there is not enough evidence to determine whether MHT affects dementia risk.

Amen agreed that there is not enough evidence to support using MHT specifically to prevent dementia. He said hormonal changes during menopause may affect mood and memory, although the relationship between MHT and dementia risk remains uncertain.
'I'M A NEUROLOGIST — HERE'S WHY DEMENTIA IS RISING AND HOW TO REDUCE YOUR RISK’

"For women, as they go through menopause, lower progesterone makes them anxious, and [with] lower estrogen, they start to have memory problems," he said. "Hormone replacement early on is helpful, and that's what we see on the brain imaging work that we do."
Experts note that while menopause-related hormonal changes can be associated with mood and cognitive symptoms, these effects can vary widely.
Stroke
A stroke occurs when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or when a blood vessel in or near the brain bursts, according to the American Stroke Association.
Conditions that affect the heart and blood vessels can also affect brain health and are associated with a higher risk of dementia, according to Amen.
Any blood flow blockages can impact brain health and increase the risk of dementia. (iStock)
That can include conditions such as heart disease, heart rhythm problems, stroke and transient ischemic attacks. Erectile dysfunction can also be associated with underlying vascular disease, he said.
"And 40% of 40-year-olds have erectile dysfunction, 70% of 70-year-olds. So, if I'm an older person, I'm thinking if I get my brain right, my love life could be better, too," Amen added.
Traumatic brain injury (TBI)
Amen surmised that the WHO is "late to the party" in emphasizing the importance of head trauma as a dementia risk factor. TBI can range from a mild concussion to a severe brain injury.
COMMON VACCINE LINKED TO 24% LOWER DEMENTIA RISK IN OLDER ADULTS

"One of the big lessons from the brain imaging work we do is that mild traumatic brain injury ruins people's lives," he said. "They end up seeing psychiatrists because they have temper problems or ... depression or anxiety, and it's really from a snowmobiling accident in [their] 30s."
Amen added that failing to protect the brain — which he described as "very soft" and having the consistency of "soft butter" — is "not the smart thing to do."
"Mild traumatic brain injury ruins people's lives," the brain expert said. (iStock)
Vision impairment
A significant portion of the brain is dedicated to vision, according to Amen.
"So, if your vision becomes troubled, your brain's troubled," he said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Amen said vision impairment may place additional demands on the brain. While the condition has been linked with cognitive decline, the WHO says there is insufficient evidence to recommend vision treatment specifically for dementia prevention.
Sleep disorders
Sleep appears to support the brain’s waste-clearance processes, Amen noted.
Sleep challenges affect tens of millions of Americans. In 2024, 30.5% of U.S. adults reported getting less than seven hours of shut-eye per day, according to the CDC.
For those with sleep problems such as sleep apnea, it can cause changes in the brain that resemble the hallmarks of Alzheimer’s disease, the expert said.
Research suggests that sleep may help the brain clear beta-amyloid, although the relationship between sleep and dementia remains complex and is still being studied.
HIV
Inflammation and infections can affect brain health. Untreated HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) can affect the central nervous system and is associated with HIV-related cognitive impairment.
"If you love and care for your brain, you're going to love your life a whole bunch more."
Amen said he has scanned "hundreds of people" with HIV, stating that the virus is "clearly a risk factor."

Untreated HIV is known to affect the central nervous system and is associated with HIV-related cognitive impairment. Effective antiretroviral therapy has greatly reduced the incidence of severe HIV-associated dementia.
Air pollution
Exposure to any toxins, from alcohol and marijuana to lead, mercury or air pollution, could be detrimental to brain health, according to Amen.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The WHO recommends reducing exposure to household and outdoor air pollution, particularly fine particulate matter. Research has linked long-term exposure to air pollution with a higher risk of cognitive decline and dementia, although the WHO characterizes the evidence as low to very low certainty.
Exposure to any toxins, from alcohol and marijuana to lead, mercury or air pollution, is detrimental to brain health, the doctor warned. (iStock)
Getting ahead of it
Dementia risk rises sharply with age. A recent U.S. analysis estimated that about one in five people had developed dementia by age 85, with risk increasing further at older ages.
While those with a genetic predisposition to the disease have a higher risk, Amen noted that certain lifestyle factors can increase the risk for anyone.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"We should be on a dementia prevention program our whole lives," the doctor said. "It’s not something to start when you're 65."
Amen urged everyone to ask themselves the question: "Is what I’m doing good or bad for my brain?"
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Social activity is one of the prevention strategies. New learning is a prevention strategy," he added. "So always working on being connected with other people and then just making better decisions."
"If you love and care for your brain, you're going to love your life a whole bunch more."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Popular artificial sweetener linked to potentially dangerous heart risk
summary: A new study of over 17,700 participants links higher xylitol blood levels to increased cardiovascular risk, including heart attack and stroke, over future decades.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to discuss a new study suggesting low sugar intake before age two leads to a reduced risk of developing dementia.
People who consume greater amounts of a popular artificial sweetener could face a greater risk of heart attack and stroke, a new study suggests.

The research, which was presented at the ESC Cardiology Congress in Germany this week, showed that higher levels of xylitol in the blood were associated with an increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE).

Xylitol is a sugar alcohol that is commonly used as a low-calorie sweetener and sugar substitute, according to the National Institutes of Health. It is often used in higher amounts to sweeten foods, drinks, chewing gum and dental care products.
ZERO-CALORIE SWEETENERS COULD ALTER THE GENES OF LATER GENERATIONS, NEW STUDY WARNS
The researchers followed two large study cohorts of more than 17,700 Canadian and British participants.

Over a six-year follow-up, people in the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging with the highest xylitol levels had a 57% higher risk of death, myocardial infarction or stroke related to cardiovascular events compared to those with the lowest levels.
People who consume greater amounts of a popular artificial sweetener could face a greater risk of heart attack and stroke, a new study suggests. (iStock)
Over 30 years, participants in the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer (EPIC)-Norfolk group with the highest xylitol levels had an 18% greater risk of MACE.
Both cohorts showed evidence of a dose-dependent association, in which higher blood xylitol concentrations corresponded to higher rates of cardiovascular events.
DIRTY SODA DRINKS ARE EVERYWHERE, BUT DOCTORS WARN OF HEALTH RISKS: 'METABOLIC DISASTER'
These higher risks persisted even after the researchers adjusted for other factors like age, gender, body mass index, hypertension, diabetes and lipid levels.

The study follows previous research that showed xylitol can enhance the ability of platelets to form clots, according to Dr. Marco Witkowski, the study presenter from Charité University Hospital in Berlin, Germany.
Xylitol is a sugar alcohol that is commonly used as a low-calorie sweetener and sugar substitute. (iStock)
"Artificial sweeteners are consumed by people who think they are healthier than sugar, and they are generally regarded as safe by regulatory agencies," the doctor said in a statement.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Our long-term findings in the general population highlight how little we know about the cardiovascular safety of xylitol and indicate that further studies are warranted, especially as the amount of xylitol in products continues to increase."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The study was observational and does not prove that xylitol causes cardiovascular events, as the researchers noted that more studies are needed to confirm the findings.

The report also does not establish whether high levels of xylitol in the blood necessarily reflect dietary consumption, as the sugar alcohol can also be produced naturally in the body as part of glucose metabolism.
People with the highest xylitol levels had a 57% higher risk of death, myocardial infarction or stroke related to cardiovascular events compared to those with the lowest levels. (iStock)

"These disturbing findings with [a] plausible mechanism of xylitol increasing cardiovascular risk should be taken very seriously," Dr. Aseem Malhotra, a cardiologist and public health campaigner based in London, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"As a practicing cardiologist, I see many patients suffering from anxiety and palpitations that resolve as soon as they stop taking artificial sweeteners."
Malhotra, who was not involved in the study, noted that one of the most important dietary changes to reduce cardiovascular risk is to "unsweeten your sweet tooth."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"That’s why I advise all my patients to avoid all processed sugars and artificial sweeteners for six weeks to break the addiction," he added.
Fox News Digital reached out to several food and beverage trade groups for comment.
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Dietitian reveals simple eating strategy for better sleep — and one habit to avoid
summary: Tart cherry juice tops a dietitian's list of sleep-boosting foods, with its natural melatonin content shown to improve both sleep quality and quantity.
story: The New Jersey-based registered dietitian and certified diabetes care specialist says certain foods can make, or break, a good night’s sleep, while a common habit can interfere with rest.
How you eat can influence how you sleep, according to experts.
Erin Palinski-Wade, a New Jersey-based registered dietitian, certified diabetes care specialist and author of "The Sleepdemic Solution," says certain foods can make, or break, a good night’s sleep.
"There are a number of foods that can help support sleep, and sometimes it's even a combination," she told Fox News Digital.
5-STEP SLEEP RESET COULD PROMOTE HEALTHY WEIGHT LOSS, NUTRITIONIST SAYS
Supporting better sleep
Keeping blood sugar steady throughout the day may help prevent afternoon energy crashes and support more restorative sleep at night, Palinski-Wade said.
Waking up in the middle of the night and struggling to fall back asleep may not always be insomnia, she suggested, but could be linked to fluctuations in glucose levels.
Keeping blood sugar steady throughout the day may help prevent afternoon energy crashes and support more restorative sleep at night. (iStock)
Combining lean proteins, slow-digesting carbohydrates and healthy fats in meals and snacks can help stabilize those levels — what Palinski-Wade called the "No. 1 way" to improve overall sleep.
Some small studies suggest tart cherry juice may support sleep, and the expert named tart cherries — or 100% tart cherry juice — as her top choice.
FOOD CRAVINGS AT 3:45 PM AREN'T RANDOM, HERE'S WHAT YOUR BODY MAY BE WARNING YOU ABOUT

"Tart cherries [are] one of the foods that have the highest amount of melatonin naturally, but they also have compounds that help to really extend that melatonin in our bodies and our body's ability to use it," she said.
Still, research linking tart cherry consumption to modest improvements in sleep duration or quality is limited and mixed; a 2025 systematic review reached a similar conclusion.
The expert recommends ingesting 4 to 6 ounces of 100% tart cherry juice or about a quarter cup of dried tart cherries for better sleep. (iStock)
For those who suffer from insomnia, Palinski-Wade recommends ingesting 4 to 6 ounces of 100% tart cherry juice, or about a quarter cup of dried tart cherries.
"It's a really, really great tool to improve your sleep – and it's really tasty, too," she said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Foods and drinks that may help reduce inflammation can also support sleep, the dietitian said.
"When we have more antioxidants in the body, more anti-inflammatory compounds, we're really helping our body to achieve that more restful state," Palinski-Wade said.
Foods rich in antioxidants and anti-inflammatory compounds — including nuts and seeds, olive oil and avocados — also provide healthy fats and other nutrients that may support sleep.
Any more than 300 milligrams of caffeine per day becomes a "stressor to our body," the expert warned. (iStock)
Caffeine’s sleep impact
On the other hand, Palinski-Wade warned that caffeine intake can negatively impact sleep quality.

"So many of us have a poor night's sleep and the next day we reach for caffeine to give us a burst of energy," she said. "And there's nothing wrong with a little bit of caffeine, but you have to look at how much you're having and how close to bedtime."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"And it's a stimulant, so it's harder to fall asleep," Palinski-Wade warned. "If you have foods or beverages with a large amount of caffeine, and you're having them in the afternoon or toward the evening, that is going to make it very hard to get restorative, restful sleep in the evening."
For those who do drink caffeine, it is best to stop about 10 hours before bedtime, the expert advised.
Stimulation and inflammation from caffeine can disrupt sleep if consumed too close to bedtime. (iStock)
The "sweet spot" for daily caffeine intake is 300 milligrams or less, she said. Any more than that becomes a "stressor to our body." A cup of coffee, traditionally 8 ounces, is about 100 milligrams.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The FDA says up to 400 milligrams daily is not generally associated with negative effects for most adults, although individual tolerance can vary depending on factors such as medications, health conditions and sensitivity to caffeine.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"We start to release stress hormones like cortisol and adrenaline, and that not only makes our body store fat versus burn it, but it also increases inflammation," Palinski-Wade noted.
"So now you have the stimulant, you have this inflammation, and all those things go against quality sleep."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Why Dolly Parton’s death can feel like losing someone you knew personally
summary: Fans worldwide describe "post-Parton depression" as Dolly Parton's death triggers intense parasocial grief that psychologists say mirrors real loss.
story: Dolly Parton, the Grammy-winning singer, songwriter and philanthropist whose career spanned over six decades, has died at 80.
The death of Dolly Parton has prompted an outpouring of grief from fans around the world, many of whom have shared that they feel like they’ve lost someone they knew personally.

Grief experts say it’s possible to experience genuine feelings of loss even if there wasn’t a personal relationship — particularly when the public figure has become woven into people’s memories and routines over a long period of time.
Psychologists refer to this type of loss as parasocial grief, according to licensed clinical psychologist Dr. Dara Houp.
DOLLY PARTON’S PRIVATE CANCER BATTLE HIGHLIGHTS WHY SOME PATIENTS DON’T SHARE THEIR DIAGNOSES

"When a celebrity shares their personal life – childhood experiences, hardships and victories – our brains register these bits of information through the same emotional and neural pathways utilized for our real-life friendships and a genuine attachment is developed," Houp, with Pathways Psychological Services in New York City, told Fox News Digital.
When that perceived relationship comes to an end, people may experience the parasocial grief, she said.

\Fans of Dolly Parton visit a mural featuring her likeness in the city's North Side on Aug. 26, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. Fans across the nation are mourning the death of the country music star, actress and philanthropist who died on Tuesday at age 80. (Getty Images)

Desiree Taranto, a licensed mental health counselor and clinical director at Empower Your Mind Therapy in New York City, said the widespread reaction also reflects "collective grief," a shared emotional response when a loss resonates across a community.
"Parton’s music, movies, philanthropy and public persona became part of many people’s family traditions, memories and difficult life moments," she told Fox News Digital.
Fans share their grief

"I honestly didn’t know I could react that way over someone I don’t even personally know," one user wrote in a grief support group on Reddit. "[Dolly] was a ray of sunshine in this dark world nowadays, and I just can’t help but cry and get so emotional about it."
Another user shared that "as each day passes, losing Dolly seems to hurt more instead of less. I have found myself crying and feeling this deep sadness that I just can’t shake."
IN WAKE OF DOLLY PARTON'S DEATH, ONCOLOGIST REVEALS WHY SOME PATIENTS KEEP CANCER DIAGNOSES SECRET
"I never met Dolly, and I know she didn’t know me, but I loved her for most of my life. That love was real, and so this grief feels real too."
Someone else in a different group referred to the feelings of sadness as "post-Parton depression."
Fans honor Dolly Parton with flowers, notes and small gifts at the site of her star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame on Aug. 26, 2026 in Hollywood, California. (Getty Images)
"I don't know why I am taking Dolly Parton's death so hard," one user wrote. "I never met her… She didn't know me. But for some reason, I can't stop crying."
"I think the reason it's hard is because she was a light and just a wonderful human," someone else shared. "She is exactly who Jesus wanted us to be."
Why does it feel personal?
The emotions people experience when grieving a celebrity can feel as real as those felt after losing someone they knew personally, Houp said.

"Perceived relational intimacy, not whether we actually know an individual, is largely what determines the intensity of grief," she said. "The emotional connection your brain developed runs along the same neural pathways as real-life bonds."
"Accept your feelings and know that it is okay to mourn someone you never met."

It’s also possible that the deaths of certain celebrities — particularly those associated with childhood, family traditions or major life moments — are more likely to trigger an intense grief response, the expert noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"When a celebrity’s life is connected to a personal milestone — such as a break-up or the birth of a child — their death permanently disrupts a living connection to who, what or where you used to be," Houp said. "Losing a celebrity can feel like losing a piece of your own history."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
A song may be tied to someone who has died, a family memory or a difficult period when Parton’s work brought comfort, Taranto noted, making the loss feel connected to a person’s own life story.
Over decades in the public eye, Parton gave fans a window into her life, allowing them to form a sense of who she was, Houp said.
Fans pay tribute to Dolly Parton at her home in Brentwood on Aug. 25, 2026 in Brentwood, Tennessee. (Getty Images)
"For many who followed Dolly’s life, she represented resilience and ambition, authenticity and bold self-expression, and a rare, unconditional kindness," she said.
"We identified with the goodness we saw in Dolly and felt encouraged by her ability to overcome hardship – thereby furthering our sense of connection to her."
Tips to navigate grief
Taranto offered advice for those feeling the grief following Parton’s death.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Accept your feelings and know that it is okay to mourn someone you never met," she said. "Do not judge yourself or feel embarrassed because that person’s work, values or advocacy touched your life personally."
It can also help to reach out to others who are also grieving the loss.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Be there for each other and allow others to be there for you," Taranto advised. "Tell stories, listen to her music, watch her movies or journal about what she meant to you."
"Remember the positive impact she made in the world and the ways she used her platform for good. Shared grief can help us process a loss because it reminds us that we are not alone in it."
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Drug institute warns that Trump-shaped ecstasy pills contain potentially fatal ingredient
summary: The Trimbos Institute in the Netherlands issued a red alert after Donald Trump-shaped ecstasy pills containing potentially fatal PMMA were handed in at testing centers.
story: President Donald Trump highlighted a massive drop in fentanyl deaths and illegal drugs entering the country by sea in an exclusive interview with Trace Gallagher.
A respected drug treatment and mental health center in the Netherlands issued a warning against taking ecstasy pills shaped like President Donald Trump’s head, saying they could be fatal.

The Trimbos Institute warned in a "red alert" that the pills contain a high concentration of PMMA, also known as para-methoxymethamphetamine, which is similar to ecstasy’s active ingredient MDMA but is slower acting.
The slow onset could encourage users to take more and potentially overdose.
The institute shared a photo of two of the pills, one of which was green on the front and the other yellow. They were red and blue on the back.
POLICE SEIZE COCAINE BRICKS WITH STICKERS OF NORWEGIAN SOCCER STAR ERLING HAALAND ALL OVER THEM

This undated photo provided by the Trimbos Institute of Mental Health and Addiction shows pills with a depiction of President Donald Trump on one side and NL and Trump stamped on the other. (Trimbos Institute of Mental Health and Addiction via AP)
The pills had a likeness of Trump’s face on the front and the name "Trump" and letters "NL" on the back.
"Absolutely do not use these pills," the institute said.
In 2018, Indiana State police seized orange Trump-shaped ecstasy pills in an operation targeting small-time drug traffickers.
Those pills also had Trump’s face on the front and "great again" written on the back, an apparent reference to his Make America Great Again slogan.
The institute said the pills have a slow-acting ingredient that could lead to overdose. (Trimbos Institute of Mental Health and Addiction via AP)
In 2017, German police also seized thousands of Trump-shaped ecstasy pills, which also appeared to be orange, that had an estimated street value of nearly $46,000.
There have yet to be any reports of overdoses or deaths due to the drug, spokesperson Anniek Groothuis told The Associated Press.
GERMAN POLICE SEIZE THOUSANDS OF 'TRUMP' ECSTASY TABLETS
"We do not know of any victims where PMMA was found in their blood," she said.
Indiana State Police released a photo showing ecstasy pills bearing President Trump's image and the words "great again" in 2018. (Indiana State Police )
The clinic said the pills had recently been handed in to some of its centers where it tests drugs before people take them.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
While ecstasy is illegal in the Netherlands, hundreds of thousands of people use the drug every year, according to the government.
Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

title: ‘Quiet quitting’ in marriage: The subtle signs a spouse has emotionally checked out
summary: Licensed therapist Lisa Brookes Kift outlines how "quiet quitting" erodes marriages and why the absence of arguing may signal emotional detachment.
story: Dr. Anna Elton discusses why stressed partners may lose interest in physical affection and how regular check-ins, gratitude and intentional time together can change the dynamic at home.
"Quiet quitting," a workplace term for doing only the minimum required, has also been used to describe a pattern in some marriages.
In relationships, the informal term refers to spouses who remain together while reducing their emotional effort, communication or involvement in the relationship.
Couples may continue managing day-to-day responsibilities, such as household tasks and parenting, even as one partner becomes emotionally and physically disengaged, relationship experts say.
‘NO CONTACT’ ON THE RISE: NEARLY 2 IN 5 AMERICANS CUT TIES WITH LOVED ONES
Discussion of the term has gained traction on social media, with users sharing videos and posts about remaining in a marriage while feeling checked out.
Licensed marriage and family therapist Lisa Brookes Kift of Marin Therapy and Counseling in California told Fox News Digital that a noticeable absence of friction can be an early warning sign.
A couple lying in bed and looking at their cellular phones, ignoring each other (iStock)

"It’s a myth that an absence of arguing in a relationship automatically means the relationship is healthy," Kift said. "Many are conflict-avoidant and rather than address their feelings, opt to sweep them under the rug, which over the long term erodes the foundation of emotional safety."
Kift said a person’s attachment style — patterns of seeking closeness and support in relationships — can influence how they respond to marital distress.
CUT OFF BY YOUR ADULT CHILD? PSYCHOLOGY RESEARCHER REVEALS WHAT PARENTS SHOULD DO NEXT
"An avoidant style may be more able to stay in their own lane — on their own island — to ride it out, because they are most comfortable resourcing in themselves," she said.

Those with a more secure attachment style are less likely to stay in that dynamic because they may be more inclined to give a partner the benefit of the doubt and believe problems can be worked through, the expert noted.
Early lessons about trust, worthiness and whether personal needs will be met heavily influence how a partner handles marital distress. (bymuratdeniz via Getty Images)
These patterns can be shaped, in part, by early experiences involving trust, worthiness and whether a person’s emotional needs were met, according to Kift.
"What did they learn about whether their needs would be met? Whether the most important people to them could be trusted? That they were lovable for who they were and not what they did?" Kift asked.
When adult relationships appear to repeat those early disappointments, partners can lose hope, she added.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"I’ve seen quite a few people in my therapy practice who have taken this stance, where there have been failed attempts to get emotional and other needs met, leading to hopelessness," Kift said.
Kift identified several early signs that a partner may be becoming emotionally disengaged.
Decline in open communicationUnresolved conflictsGrowing impatienceA tendency to assume the worst about a spouse's intentions rather than giving them the benefit of the doubt
Decline in open communication
Unresolved conflicts
Growing impatience
A tendency to assume the worst about a spouse's intentions rather than giving them the benefit of the doubt

Left unaddressed, the relationship could shift into what journalist Monica Corcoran Harel described on Oprah’s podcast as "parallel play," a reference to toddlers playing side by side without meaningfully engaging with one another.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Repairing a marriage requires both partners to reengage, Kift said, which can be difficult once one spouse has become deeply emotionally detached.
Signs like reduced communication, unresolved arguments, growing impatience and assuming the worst about a partner’s intentions can signal an impending emotional slide. (iStock)

"If one has fully checked out, they will not be open to repair," she said, adding that hypervigilance — remaining on guard for hurt or disappointment — can make it difficult for a person to recognize positive changes in their partner.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
For couples willing to work on the relationship, Kift suggests starting with a conversation that feels safe and communicates care.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
As one example, she suggested saying, "I know it may not have looked like it, but you and our marriage are very important to me. Can we find a time to sit down and talk?"
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Measles deaths may have been 'fabricated,' RFK Jr claims after coroner raises questions
summary: RFK Jr. alleged Pennsylvania's two measles-associated deaths may have been "fabricated" as a dispute with Gov. Josh Shapiro over the outbreak intensifies.
story: CNN's Dana Bash sparred with HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. over vaccine efficacy amid rising measles cases in the U.S. on "State of the Union" Sunday.
Days after Pennsylvania health officials reported two measles deaths, a public dispute has emerged about whether other factors played a role in the fatalities.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) confirmed the two "measles-associated" deaths on Tuesday, noting that both individuals were unvaccinated.
These were the state’s first measles-related deaths in 35 years, according to the release.
FORMER CDC ADVISOR SAYS DECLINE IN KINDERGARTEN VACCINATIONS NOTHING TO WORRY ABOUT: 'KEEP CALM AND CARRY ON'

That confirmation came after the county coroner — physician Stephen Diamantoni — said the newborn died shortly after birth from a lacerated spleen and had tested positive for measles acquired before birth, according to The Philadelphia Inquirer.
Days after Pennsylvania health officials reported two measles deaths, a public dispute has emerged about whether other factors played a role in the fatalities. (iStock)
Diamantoni’s office was still investigating the newborn’s death, and the coroner said he was not aware of the other reported death, Axios reported.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health stated that not all deaths are referred to a coroner under state law.

The DOH says it uses the term "measles-associated" when laboratory or epidemiologic evidence of measles is present, even if a coroner or medical certifier does not identify measles as the immediate cause of death.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) confirmed two "measles-associated" deaths on Tuesday, noting that both individuals were unvaccinated. (iStock)
Measles can affect the spleen, potentially causing enlargement and, in rare cases, rupture, according to Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News senior medical analyst.
Pregnant women, newborns and young infants can face a higher risk of serious measles complications, the doctor noted.
Infants who are too young to receive the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccine can be especially vulnerable.
COMMON VACCINE LINKED TO 24% LOWER DEMENTIA RISK IN OLDER ADULTS
HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has questioned whether Pennsylvania officials provided sufficient information to substantiate the two measles-associated deaths.

In a Wednesday post on X, after the coroner’s comments were made public, Kennedy alleged that Pennsylvania had not given the CDC relevant information and suggested the deaths could have been "fabricated."
Measles can affect the spleen, potentially causing enlargement and, in rare cases, rupture, according to Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News senior medical analyst. (iStock)

"The announcement appears to have been premature, and the deaths may even have been altogether fabricated by one of the Governor's hopeful staffers," he wrote. "The Lancaster County Coroner says that it has no record of any measles deaths."
RFK also accused Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and his office of "fearmongering, misinformation, finger-pointing and the weaponization of infectious disease fears for political gain."
"The Lancaster County Coroner says that it has no record of any measles deaths."
Meanwhile, at a Tuesday press conference, Shapiro said the deaths showed the "real-life consequences" of misinformation about the measles vaccine.
In a subsequent X post, the governor claimed Kennedy had "stoked confusion amongst parents and others — and the result has been less protection from measles and more cases."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

In response to Kennedy’s comments, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention also spoke on X about the debate, expressing appreciation for RFK’s efforts to "clarify conflicting information" about the cause of the two reported deaths.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"CDC is working to determine what actually occurred," the agency wrote. "These discrepancies raise important questions, particularly because the Governor’s Office has not provided CDC with information relevant to the outbreak and has declined our offers of assistance."
"Under President Trump’s and Secretary Kennedy’s leadership, CDC will follow the facts and tell the American people the truth."
HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has questioned whether Pennsylvania officials provided sufficient information to substantiate the two measles-associated deaths. (REUTERS/Elizabeth Frantz)
Pennsylvania Health Secretary Dr. Debra Bogen disputed the CDC’s account, saying the two deaths were reported to the agency’s measles response team early Tuesday morning.

In an X post from the Pennsylvania Department of Health account, Bogen said she had reviewed the case investigations and that state epidemiologists had thoroughly investigated both deaths. She confirmed that both individuals tested positive for measles.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Meanwhile, Lancaster County Commissioner Josh Parsons said he did not believe there was enough evidence to confirm the two deaths were caused by measles, citing information he said he received from the county coroner’s office, according to Local21 News.
What does ‘measles-associated’ mean?
Siegel noted that measles weakens the immune system and increases the risk of pneumonia, which can stem from measles itself or from a secondary bacterial infection.

When a patient has both measles and another immediate cause of death, several considerations come into play when infectious disease specialists are determining whether the virus was a contributing factor. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
"If the impact of measles on the immune system or stress on other major organs as a result of the disease leads to death, that would be a measles-associated death," he told Fox News Digital.

When a patient has both measles and another immediate cause of death, several considerations come into play when infectious disease specialists are determining whether the virus was a contributing factor.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"It has to do with whether the immediate cause of death is from measles itself, as in measles pneumonia, or due to damage to the immune system and secondary infections or other diseases that result," Siegel said.
Lancaster County is at the center of Pennsylvania’s current measles outbreak. As of Friday, the state had reported 424 confirmed cases and 73 hospitalizations.
Fox News Digital reached out to RFK Jr. and other officials requesting comment.

title: Common vaccine linked to 24% lower dementia risk in older adults
summary: A Brown University study found Shingrix reduced dementia risk by 24% over four years, building on prior research linking the shingles vaccine to brain health.
story: Neurologist Dr. Ajeet Sodhi breaks down research linking the shingles vaccine to a reduced risk of dementia, while stressing that the findings show an association, not proof that the vaccine treats dementia.
A recent study led by researchers at Brown University appears to strengthen the link between shingles vaccination and a reduced risk of dementia diagnoses in older adults.

The study, published in The Annals of Internal Medicine, evaluated electronic health records and Medicare claims for more than 509,926 U.S. adults 66 and older who were admitted to skilled nursing facilities.

Individuals who received at least one dose of the recombinant shingles vaccine, commercially known as Shingrix, experienced a 24% relative reduction in dementia risk over a four-year period compared to people who did not receive the shot, the researchers found.
ALZHEIMER'S RISK MAY BE 35% LOWER WITH COMMON MENOPAUSE TREATMENT, STUDY FINDS
However, the findings show an association and do not prove that the vaccine directly prevents dementia, the researchers noted.

Dr. Ajeet Sodhi, a clinical neurologist and neuro-interventionalist in Orlando, Florida, noted that while the finding is "remarkable," it builds upon a growing foundation of scientific literature rather than standing alone.
Independent neurologist Dr. Ajeet Sodhi noted that these findings align with recent studies suggesting a link between shingles vaccines and slower cognitive decline. (iStock)

"This is maybe the third or fourth study, and they all came to the same conclusion," Sodhi, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital. "It seems that by giving patients the shingles vaccine called Shingrix, in the next couple of years, we see a clinically significant decline in the development of dementia."

Researchers have proposed several possible explanations for the association, including the vaccine's role in preventing shingles and its potential complications. The virus has also been linked to vascular events such as stroke, which can contribute to vascular dementia.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Sodhi noted that recent medical literature continues to support larger cardiovascular benefits as well.

"In addition to the study that we're talking about today, there was a study published just this week that showed the shingles vaccine results in a clinically significant reduction in the incidence of both cardiovascular disease and cerebrovascular disease," he told Fox News Digital.
"So that's heart attacks and strokes."
"The common theme in all of this is the sooner you seek evaluation, the better it is for the treatment."
The neurologist emphasized that while the data shows a strong correlation, the vaccine is not currently classified as a direct therapeutic treatment for cognitive decline.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"It's not at this time considered a treatment," he noted. "This association is ... very, very suggestive, but we can't say one-to-one it proves that this treats dementia. And this finding, honestly, is kind of like icing on the cake."
Beyond potential brain health benefits, the primary purpose of the FDA-approved vaccine is to prevent painful shingles reactivations and long-term nerve damage. (iStock)
Shingles is caused by the varicella-zoster virus, the same virus responsible for chickenpox, according to Mayo Clinic.
After a person recovers from chickenpox, the virus lies dormant in nerve tissue near the brain and spinal cord, where it can reactivate decades later as a painful rash with fluid-filled blisters.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The primary function of the vaccine remains the prevention of the severe nerve pain and rash caused by shingles reactivation.
Shingles can lead to severe complications, including post-herpetic neuralgia, a debilitating condition causing long-term nerve pain that persists after the rash clears, according to Cleveland Clinic.
The FDA recommends the two-dose Shingrix series for adults 50 and older, with specialists emphasizing that early medical assessment is critical for managing cognitive health. (iStock)

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends two doses of Shingrix for adults 50 and older, as well as adults 19 and older who are or will be immunocompromised. The vaccine is FDA-approved to prevent shingles and related complications — not to prevent or treat dementia.
The study received funding from GSK, the maker of Shingrix; the authors stated that the company had no role in the study’s design, analysis or publication.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
For individuals concerned about memory loss or family medical history, experts recommend consulting a doctor early.

"The common theme in all of this is the sooner you seek evaluation, the better it is for the treatment," Sodhi advised. "The treatment is more likely to work the earlier you are in the onset of the disease."

title: Popular weight-loss strategy shows surprising potential for chronic pain relief
summary: A study reveals that intermittent fasting reshapes the gut microbiome to strengthen the intestinal lining and block inflammatory compounds from the brain.
story: Dr. Daniel Amen, a California-based psychiatrist and founder of Amen Clinics, shares how changing the brain can help defeat chronic pain, as shared in his new book, "Change Your Brain, Change Your Pain."
Intermittent fasting has grown in popularity as a weight-loss strategy, but it could also unlock new ways to manage chronic pain by altering how the gut communicates with the brain.

A study published in the journal Brain, Behavior, and Immunity, revealed that the timing of meals affects the gut-brain axis, which is a communication system linking the gastrointestinal tract and the central nervous system.
Intermittent fasting is an eating pattern that focuses on when meals are consumed, typically involving extended periods without food, according to health institutions.
DAILY EATING HABIT LINKED TO BETTER BRAIN HEALTH IN OLDER ADULTS, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS
Chronic pain, defined by the Cleveland Clinic as pain persisting for longer than three months, is often accompanied by cognitive difficulties and anxiety.

While traditional treatments target inflammation or pain-signaling nerves, the new research suggests that meal timing may also influence chronic pain by changing gut bacteria and inflammation throughout the body.
Chronic pain is defined as pain lasting longer than three months, according to medical institutions. (iStock)

Scientists at Zhengzhou University in China examined animal models during fasting cycles. They found that intermittent fasting strengthens the intestinal lining, which prevents inflammatory compounds from leaking into the bloodstream and reaching nervous system tissue.
SECRET TO WEIGHT LOSS MAY BE HIDING IN YOUR GUT, NEW STUDY SUGGESTS

Analysis of the gut microbiome found that fasting increased levels of a bacterium called Alistipes finegoldii. When researchers administered the live bacteria to animals that were not fasting, they saw similar improvements in pain and cognitive function.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DIET SHOWS SURPRISING IMPACT ON SERIOUS MENTAL HEALTH CONDITION
The researchers found that the bacterium produces compounds that the body can convert into hippuric acid, a chemical messenger linked to the observed benefits.

Fasting increased levels of the gut bacterium Alistipes finegoldii. When researchers gave the bacterium to animals that were not fasting, they saw similar improvements in pain and cognitive function. (iStock)

At the cellular level, hippuric acid acts on an inflammatory pathway called STING, short for Stimulator of Interferon Genes. When this pathway becomes overactive in the nervous system, it can fuel inflammation that worsens pain and interferes with brain function.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The study demonstrated that hippuric acid turns down STING activity, quieting inflammatory signaling in the central nervous system and resolving behavioral symptoms.
Despite the findings, the research carries a few limitations, the research team acknowledged.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
First, observational and early-stage studies can identify a link between intermittent fasting and changes in gut-brain signaling, but they cannot prove that fasting directly causes those changes.
Because the findings are based on animal models, large-scale human clinical trials are still needed to determine safe, effective fasting protocols for chronic pain management. (iStock)
Also, individual responses to intermittent fasting vary based on each person's gut microbiome, underlying health conditions, daily nutrient intake and genetics.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
It can also be challenging for some people to adhere to fasting protocols, as strict eating windows may not be safe or feasible for everyone.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
While fasting is not a cure for chronic pain, researchers said the findings could help guide future treatments that target the gut-brain connection.
They added that further trials will be necessary to establish specific dietary protocols tailored to individual patient needs.
