title: Who pays for US power boom? Blue, red states offer starkly different ways to lower utility bills amid AI surge
summary: New Jersey is requiring big data centers to shoulder more of their own power costs, while an Indiana utility says revenue from major new customers could cut household bills by about $100 a year.
story: President Donald Trump unveils a pledge for Big Tech companies to cover AI power costs, aiming to lower consumer electricity bills. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum defends the policy, discusses the AI arms race with China and rare earth minerals.

As the AI boom drives an unprecedented hunt for electricity, two states are taking sharply different approaches to assuage fears that Big Tech’s massive energy needs will raise Americans’ utility bills.

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s approach is to set statewide ground rules before large data centers connect to the grid. Under legislation she signed in July, the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities must create a separate rate structure for large data centers and ensure that the costs of new substations, transmission lines or other grid upgrades built mainly for the data center, are not added to other customers’ bills.

The law also requires large data centers to commit to paying for at least 85% of the electricity capacity they request for a 10-year period, in case they scale back their power use or close, and it directs regulators to encourage data centers to bring clean generation or energy storage online, use power more efficiently and reduce their electricity demand during emergencies.
CHINESE BOT FARM CAUGHT RED-HANDED TRYING TO INFLUENCE HEATED AI DATA CENTER DEBATE

Sherrill has paired those ratepayer protections with new disclosure and local-planning measures. A separate law she signed this week requires operators to report their energy and water use to the state twice a year. Sherrill’s administration says the reporting and new municipal guidance will give officials a clearer picture of data centers’ demands and help communities assess local impacts and negotiate with developers.
An image of New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill and a data center, as states weigh how to manage the AI-driven surge in electricity demand while protecting household utility bills. (Getty Images)

Meanwhile, Indiana is taking a different approach. Rather than impose statewide rules for every large data center, state regulators approved a deal negotiated by Indiana Michigan Power (I&M), the Fort Wayne-based utility serving customers in Indiana and Michigan, along with consumer advocates and major technology companies.

The deal grew out of a wave of huge planned projects in I&M’s service area. Amazon Web Services (AWS) announced an $11 billion data-center campus near New Carlisle, Indiana, in 2024, while Google announced a $2 billion project in Fort Wayne. I&M and state officials then had to determine who would cover the cost of the additional power and grid infrastructure needed to serve those projects.
FROM NETFLIX TO GPS: 10 WAYS THIS HIDDEN TECH INFRASTRUCTURE QUIETLY POWERS MODERN LIFE

According to I&M, the 2025 agreement requires new large customers, including data centers, to make long-term financial commitments to pay for the electric service they request, even if their future demand falls short of expectations. With those commitments in place, I&M says it can turn the new demand into a benefit for existing customers. The utility is now asking regulators to cut base rates by $59 million in 2027, saying revenue from large customers, including data centers, makes the reduction possible.

If the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission approves the plan, I&M says an Indiana household using 1,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity a month would save about $100 a year. The utility is also proposing to freeze all rates on customers’ monthly bills for three years, with a decision expected in June 2027 and any savings beginning that summer.

Data center development is surging across Texas, with North Texas taking the top spot in a new global ranking of the industry’s leading markets. (Mikala Compton/The Austin American-Statesman/Getty Images)

Daniel Turner, executive director of the energy advocacy group Power The Future, said Indiana’s approach was better than New Jersey’s more prescriptive framework, but argued neither state had gone far enough to ensure the AI buildout adds power to the grid rather than simply consuming it.
DSA CANDIDATE PUSHES FEDERAL AI DATA CENTER MORATORIUM WITH MICHIGAN EARLY VOTING UNDERWAY

"Indiana’s approach is definitely the better of the two," Turner told Fox News Digital. "At least Indiana is saying, ‘Hey, we don’t know where this is going, but we’re not going to put in all of the guardrails yet to stop progress from happening. Let’s work together and figure out what the solution is.’"

Turner said he would make new power generation part of the deal from the start. New Jersey’s law encourages data centers to bring clean generation or energy storage online, but Turner said facilities should be built alongside the generation needed to run them and add capacity to the broader grid.
"Every data center should be built in conjunction with the necessary power-generating facility to power it and give back to the grid," he said.

Turner posited that data centers have become a political football, with officials too often choosing sweeping restrictions or open-ended delays instead of working with utilities, developers and local communities on plans that protect ratepayers while adding needed power.
KEVIN O'LEARY DETAILS MASSIVE UTAH AI DATA CENTER TO RIVAL CHINA'S TECH DOMINANCE
"The solutions to data centers are not complicated issues to solve," he said. "They just require political will."

Protestors hold up 'Stop data centers' signs, on the day of U.S. President Donald Trump's speech at the General Motors Proving Ground, in Milford, Michigan, U.S. July 27, 2026. (Carlos Osorio/Reuters)

Protesters react as the Box Elder County Commission approves a large AI data center project in Tremonton, Utah, on May 4, 2026. Activists opposed the proposed 40,000-acre development over concerns about water use, energy demand and environmental impact. (Natalie Behring/Getty Images)

The Trump administration has already sought to turn that argument into a national model. In March, the White House announced a Ratepayer Protection Pledge signed by major technology companies, including Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and xAI, which the administration says commits the companies to cover the cost of additional electricity generation needed for AI data centers rather than pass it along to families.

Turner noted the stakes of the data-center debate extend well beyond local utility bills, arguing that the United States cannot afford to fall behind China in the race to build and control artificial intelligence.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"When you tell Americans why we have to win the AI race, look at what China did with the Wuhan flu and how they tried to lie about that," Turner said. "Now imagine they can do that with every single piece of intellectual property on every platform in real time. That alone should scare the crap out of Americans."
Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: Army Secretary Dan Driscoll submits resignation to Trump
summary: Army Secretary Dan Driscoll has submitted his resignation letter to the White House, a senior U.S. official confirms. The White House has not yet accepted his resignation.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
Army Secretary Dan Driscoll has submitted his resignation to President Donald Trump, a senior U.S. official confirmed to Fox News.
The resignation remains pending and has not been accepted by the White House, the official said.

A source familiar with the matter told Fox News that Driscoll had raised concerns with the administration about the Army’s transformation and readiness, including his belief that Secretary of War Pete Hegseth had hindered those efforts.

"Driscoll brought up concerns with the administration surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth's blocking those efforts specifically by firing the Generals who were responsible," the source said.
TRUMP'S WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM CONSTRUCTION GETS ANOTHER LIFELINE FROM SCOTUS AMID HEATED LEGAL FIGHT
Army Secretary Dan Driscoll has submitted his resignation to President Donald Trump, a senior U.S. official confirmed to Fox News. (Tom Brenner/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Tensions reportedly intensified as Hegseth removed several senior Army leaders, including Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George.

Driscoll addressed George’s departure during an April 16 House Appropriations subcommittee hearing, recalling he was in North Carolina on vacation with his family and drove directly to the general’s home after learning that George had been asked to submit his resignation.
HEGSETH UPGRADES ABBEY GATE MARINES' VALOR AWARDS AFTER 5-YEAR DELAY: 'THOSE DAYS ARE OVER'
Driscoll is reportedly expected to leave the Pentagon in the coming days. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

PROGRESSIVE PRAISE FOR TRUMP AS WARREN BACKS PUSH TO CURB DEFENSE CONTRACTOR CEO PAYOUTS
Tensions reportedly intensified as Hegseth removed several senior Army leaders. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

title: Vance unloads on El-Sayed after Usha swipe with brutal warning: 'Way out of your league'
summary: JD Vance fired back at Abdul El-Sayed over comments about Usha Vance, telling the Michigan Senate candidate to keep his wife's name out of his mouth.
story: Vice President JD Vance implored Michigan Democratic Senate nominee to focus on policy issues instead of attacking his wife.
Vice President JD Vance urged Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed during a rally on Monday to focus on substantive policy issues instead of attacking his wife.

"I actually think that the people of Michigan think it's kind of weird when you talk about another guy's wife," Vance said at a metro Detroit rally organized by MAGA Inc., a super PAC aligned with the president.

"I think the people of Michigan would like you to talk about the public policy ideas …I think the people of Michigan would like you to talk about how you're going to protect auto workers when you're supporting every single policy that has undercut the wages and jobs of Michigan auto workers your entire life in public service."
EL-SAYED UNDER FIRE ONLINE AFTER TAKING AIM AT USHA VANCE, FEMALE TRUMP AIDE IN WEEKEND SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS

A split image shows Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, left, and Vice President JD Vance, right. El-Sayed won the Democratic primary for Michigan's open U.S. Senate seat and will face Republican Mike Rogers in the general election. (Jim Lo Scalzo-Pool/Getty Images; Finn Gomez/Getty Images)
"But whatever you want to talk about, Abdul, keep my wife's name the hell out of your mouth because she's way out of your league," the vice president added.

Vance's quip was in response to El-Sayed saying "do we think JD is taking Usha with him back in time to meet Papaw, or no" after the vice president suggested that Sharia law would have been an alien concept to his grandfather.

Critics said the post appeared to take aim at Usha Vance’s Indian heritage. El-Sayed later said his point was that Vance seemed to be suggesting some people are "more American" than others because their families have been in the country longer, noting that Vance’s own in-laws are immigrants.
"If you’re a rural White American living in Michigan, just remember El-Sayed believes you’re a racist," conservative commentator Ryan Girdusky said in response to the Democratic hopeful’s statement.

title: Trump's White House ballroom construction gets another lifeline from SCOTUS amid heated legal fight
summary: Chief Justice John Roberts warned the White House ballroom project is "likely unlawful," but the Supreme Court let construction continue for now.
story: Fox News correspondent Lucas Tomlinson joins 'Fox News Sunday' to discuss President Donald Trump's continuation of ballroom construction after the Supreme Court's temporary order. Tomlinson also discusses the Freedom 250 Grand Prix race in Washington, D.C., and the president's economic campaign against the Iranian regime.
The Supreme Court has again sided with the Trump administration, allowing construction on the White House ballroom project to continue while the case continues to be litigated in the lower courts.

The court split 5-4 in granting the emergency request. The decision replaces a temporary order Chief Justice John Roberts issued just hours before a lower-court ruling blocking the work was set to take effect. The underlying litigation will continue in the lower courts, but court documents indicate key parts of the project could be completed within months, potentially outpacing the legal process.
Trump quickly celebrated the decision, declaring that the high court had cleared the way for the massive project to move forward "without any further contingency, doubt, or threat."
"We are living in the Golden Age of America, and this Building will be one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington, D.C.," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
TRUMP’S WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM FOES FACE ‘VERY TOUGH ARGUMENT’ AT SUPREME COURT, LEGAL EXPERTS SAY

A view of ongoing construction of the East Wing ballroom at the White House, as seen from the Washington Monument observation deck in Washington, DC on August 28, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz / AFP via Getty Images)
Trump said the "magnificent Ballroom and Military Complex" is expected to be completed in summer 2028 and predicted it will be "something that the entire Country is very proud of."
He also took a swipe at the National Trust for Historic Preservation, blasting its legal challenge as a "baseless lawsuit" and claiming the project is both under budget and ahead of schedule.
"The Ballroom is totally funded by Great Patriots and Corporations and, therefore, is a Gift — At no cost to the American Taxpayer," Trump wrote.

The president’s victory lap came as Chief Justice John Roberts issued a strongly worded dissent from the latest order, declaring that construction of the ballroom is "likely unlawful" and warning that allowing the project to proceed risks infringing on Congress’ constitutional powers.

"The President ordered the demolition of the East Wing of the White House to make way for a new, privately funded state ballroom in its place," Roberts wrote. "Construction of the ballroom has proceeded apace for the better part of a year."
APPEALS COURT SAYS FEDERAL JUDGE MUST RECONSIDER BLOCKING WH BALLROOM, WEIGH NATIONAL SECURITY CONCERNS
"That construction is likely unlawful," he wrote.
Roberts pointed to federal law that prohibits the construction of any "building or structure" on federal government parkland in Washington, D.C., without express authorization from Congress.
The chief justice argued that the ballroom falls squarely within that restriction because it is being built on President’s Park, federal land that encompasses the White House and surrounding grounds.

"The ballroom is a building or structure being erected on federal park grounds—President’s Park—in the District of Columbia," Roberts wrote. "Yet Congress has not passed any law resembling ‘express authority’ for the Executive’s construction of it."
TRUMP SAYS WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM RULING JEOPARDIZES LIVES OF FUTURE PRESIDENTS, VOWS SUPREME COURT APPEAL
Construction on the new White House ballroom is seen from the Washington Monument, Monday, April 20, 2026, in Washington. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)
The Supreme Court’s decision allows construction to continue while the underlying legal challenge plays out, but it does not settle the ultimate question of whether the ballroom project is lawful.

The case remains in litigation in the lower courts, meaning Roberts’ assertion that the construction is "likely unlawful" represents his view in dissent rather than a final determination by the Supreme Court.
DOJ CITES WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENTS' DINNER SHOOTING IN PUSH TO DROP LAWSUIT AGAINST BALLROOM
Heavy machinery tears down a section of the East Wing of the White House as construction begins on President Donald Trump's planned ballroom on October 22, 2025. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images)

Roberts also took issue with the court’s treatment of Alison Hoagland, who originally challenged the project, arguing that both the historic nature of the White House and her interest in its preservation deserved greater weight.
"The White House is not just any building, and—when it comes to historic preservation—Hoagland is not just any person," Roberts wrote.
REPUBLICANS QUESTION TRUMP'S 'PRIVATELY FUNDED' BALLROOM AFTER REPORT POINTS TO TAXPAYER BURDEN
An excavator works to clear rubble after the East Wing of the White House was demolished on Oct. 23, 2025 in Washington, D.C. (Eric Lee/Getty Images)

"In failing to appreciate as much, the Court misconceives the plaintiff’s injury, allowing the Executive’s likely infringement of the Legislature’s power of the purse and authority to regulate federal property in the District of Columbia to continue," he wrote.
"Today’s decision is no victory for the separation of powers."
Roberts closed his dissent by invoking former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and issuing a pointed warning about how decisions involving the White House are made.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Winston Churchill once remarked that ‘[w]e shape our buildings, and afterwards our buildings shape us,’" Roberts wrote.
"All the more reason to ensure that those responsible follow the rules in deciding what to tear down and what to build up at the People’s House."
"I respectfully dissent," he wrote.
In addition to Roberts, Justices Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson also dissented.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: DSA leader's working-class image takes hit as public records pile up contradictions
summary: Gustavo Gordillo, NYC Democratic Socialists of America co-chair, faces scrutiny over claims about his immigrant parents, union status and housing.
story: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is pressed on whether he still stands by embattled NYC-DSA co-chair Gustavo Gordillo amid scrutiny over Gordillo’s housing situation and work history.

The contradictions are piling up around New York City Democratic Socialists of America co-chair Gustavo Gordillo, whose claims about his working-class credentials — from being a "union electrician" to his housing and family story — have increasingly collided with public records and other evidence.
Gordillo has repeatedly invoked his family’s immigrant success story while explaining his support for socialism.

"My parents came here, they had nothing," Gordillo told the New York Times in a profile piece earlier this month. "Their first jobs were in fast food and cleaning houses. They built success in this country. And they’re absolutely the exception."
According to Gordillo, he advances the cause of socialism because he believes it can "build a world" where his parents’ success story is "not exceptional."
LUXURY TRAVEL, SHOPPING, SIX-FIGURE INCOME: BATTLEGROUND DEMS RIPPED FOR 'PHONY' WORKING-CLASS NARRATIVE

Members of the Democratic Socialists of America gather outside of a Trump-owned building during a May Day rally in New York City in 2019. (left); Gustavo Gordillo sits in-studio on "The Story With Martha MacCallum (right). (Spencer Platt/Getty Images/Fox News)
A 2021 obituary for Gordillo’s paternal grandfather, however, raises questions about the family history behind that account, the New York Post reported Saturday.

Manuel Gordillo, Gordillo’s grandfather, emigrated from Peru to the United States to practice medicine in 1958. After settling in the United States, Manuel met his future wife in St. Louis, and the couple later had Gordillo’s father, Gustavo, per the obituary.

The obituary also notes that Gordillo’s grandfather built a successful life as a psychiatrist in Ohio, at one point serving as the president of the Ohio Psychiatric Association, casting doubt on the socialist’s claim that his parents grew up in poverty.

"My dad, his first job in the United States was working at Wendy’s, my mom’s first job was a house cleaner, and they did make a living for themselves, and they had success," Gordillo told Fox News in July.

The elder Gordillo's obituary portrays him as a loving and active father, noting that he raised his "children in Lakewood, Ohio" and that "his most cherished role was as a husband, father, grandfather, and uncle/tio."

"Gustavo and his parents were born in Peru and immigrated to the US," a New York City Democratic Socialists of America spokesperson told Fox News Digital following publication. "Gustavo’s father grew up in Peru, not in the United States, and the family had limited contact with Gustavo’s grandfather, who is the subject of the Post’s recent reporting."
The New York City Democratic Socialists of America later told Fox News Digital that their co-chair's father was a product of Gordillo's first marriage.
The questions surrounding Gordillo’s account of his family history come after discrepancies emerged over how he has described his occupation and living arrangements.
DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST HEADED FOR $142K LEGISLATURE SALARY BEGS FOR RENT HANDOUT, DELETES POST AFTER BACKLASH
Members of the Democratic Socialists of America gather outside a Trump-owned building on May Day, May 1, 2019, in New York City. (Getty Images)

The 38-year-old socialist, for example, told the New York Times that he was renting a modest apartment in the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn only for it to be revealed that he was actually living in a $1.4 million townhouse owned by his father in a trendier part of the borough.

"Not only did DSA co-chair Gustavo Gordillo's parents buy him this rowhouse, they converted it from a two family and renovated it into a luxury single-family home for him," New York City Councilwoman Vickie Paladino said on X. "Exactly the kind of 'greed' the DSA rails against on a daily basis, and reducing valuable housing inventory by one more unit, which is supposedly something the DSA cares very deeply about."
FRUSTRATED BLUE-COLLAR UNION BOSSES RIP SOCIALIST POLITICIANS, WARN OF LABOR EXODUS FROM DEM PARTY

Items on a table during an election night party held by the Democratic Socialists of America - LA chapter at The Greyhound on Nov. 4, 2025 in Los Angeles. (Eric Thayer/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

Also undercutting Gordillo’s working-class image is his continued self-identification as a "union electrician" despite the fact that he hasn’t been a member of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers since March, when he was fired for not showing up to his apprenticeship.

"After learning of Mr. Gordillo’s prolonged absence from and failure to participate in required work and classes, the trustees of the Joint Apprentice Training Committee terminated Mr. Gordillo from the program," the IBEW said in a statement.

Even with the IBEW publicly stating that Gordillo is not a member of their organization, the socialist leader still identifies himself as a "union electrician" on social media.

title: El-Sayed torched online after brushing off questions about Hasan Piker campaign ties: ‘What a pal’

story: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, argues reporters are ‘missing the boat’ when asking about controversial streamer Hasan Piker.

Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed is facing a wave of online blowback after dodging questions about his ties to far-left streamer Hasan Piker, a frequent presence on the campaign trail in Michigan.

"But I don’t want to have a conversation about a Twitch streamer in California," El-Sayed said. "This is not a serious conversation."

Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed speaks to reporters on the campaign trail in Lansing, Michigan. (Fox News Digital/Paul Steinhauser)

Piker has emerged as a growing flashpoint within the Democratic Party over his past controversial remarks, including his claim that "America deserved 9/11."

title: ‘Backwards and poor’: Trump issues dire warning to communities blocking critical technology
summary: President Donald Trump warned communities rejecting data centers risk becoming "backwards and poor" as states battle over AI boom energy and water costs.
story: AI executive Brittany Kaiser explains how every time you scroll, stream or search, a data center is working behind the scenes to power your digital life.

President Donald Trump took aim Monday at the growing backlash against data centers, warning that communities that shut the door on the facilities risk missing out on the jobs and economic gains of America's AI boom.

"The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. "If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign," he added.

Trump has made energy dominance and U.S. leadership in artificial intelligence central pillars of his second term, placing data centers at the center of his push to maintain America's edge over China.
"China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement," Trump wrote, arguing that resistance to new facilities risks undercutting America's edge in the global AI race.
ELECTION WHISTLEBLOWER WARNS FOREIGN ACTORS ARE SPENDING BILLIONS TO TURN AMERICANS AGAINST AI
President Donald Trump has made energy dominance and artificial intelligence key priorities for his second term. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The data center boom has also emerged as a midterm flashpoint, as concerns over rising electricity costs, water use and rapid development collide with promises of jobs, investment and U.S. dominance in artificial intelligence.
That tension is already playing out across the country.

Trump has specifically criticized Texas Gov. Greg Abbott's approach, calling the Lone Star State's stance toward data centers a "mistake" and pointing to the economic investment the projects can bring to communities willing to host them.

Texas has cemented its status as a heavyweight in the industry, with Dallas ranking as the world's No. 1 primary data center market in Cushman & Wakefield's 2026 Global Data Center Market Comparison. But billions of dollars in new investment have also brought enormous electricity demands and questions over who should pay for the infrastructure needed to support the boom.

Abbott has moved to address those concerns, directing regulators to ensure data centers cover the infrastructure costs needed to serve them and calling on developers to add their own power generation rather than shift costs onto Texas residents.
A SOUTHERN STATE JUST TOOK THE TOP SPOT IN ONE OF THE WORLD'S FASTEST-GROWING INDUSTRIES

Texas leaders, including Gov. Greg Abbott, have sought to position the state as a destination for large-scale data center development even as officials grapple with the strain new projects could place on the electric grid. (Antranik Tavitian/Reuters)
Meanwhile, in Pennsylvania, Gov. Josh Shapiro recently imposed new requirements on large data center developments.

Other governors have taken a more restrictive stance. Democratic New York Gov. Kathy Hochul imposed a one-year moratorium on new hyper-scale data centers as states grapple with concerns over electricity costs, grid reliability and the pace of development.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Data center development is surging across the Lone Star State, with North Texas taking the top spot in a new global ranking of the industry’s leading markets. (Yasuyoshi Chiba/Contributor/AFP/Getty Images)

Data centers house the servers and computing equipment that power artificial intelligence and cloud services, requiring vast amounts of electricity to operate and cool. Most Americans may never see the inside of one, but they rely on data centers constantly, often without realizing it.

The growing patchwork of state restrictions and requirements could complicate Trump’s push for rapid data center expansion as communities weigh America’s AI ambitions against concerns over electricity costs, water use and development.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: El-Sayed tries to make peace with Jewish Democrats but draws line at dumping Hasan Piker
summary: Abdul El-Sayed met with Michigan's Democratic Jewish Caucus to apologize, but Mike Rogers calls his remarks a "sham apology" amid antisemitism concerns.
story: Asked about Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel’s criticism of his initial comments after a synagogue attack earlier this year, Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed tells Fox News Digital: ‘To anybody who feels like my comments may have been hurtful, I’m really sorry.’
Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed spent this past weekend trying to mend fences with Jewish Democrats in Michigan, but his Republican rival calls El-Sayed's comments a "sham apology."

El-Sayed, in an appearance Saturday before the Michigan Democrats' Jewish Caucus, and in an answer to a question from Fox News Digital, apologized for comments he made after a March attack on a suburban Detroit synagogue. But he pushed back when asked to repudiate controversial comments from incendiary left-wing streamer Hasan Piker, who is a strong supporter of his campaign.

A vocal critic of Israel who describes its military actions against Hamas in Gaza as "genocide," El-Sayed is facing off against former Rep. Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee in the Great Lakes battleground state, for a crucial open Senate seat the Democrats must hold in the midterm elections as they aim to win back control of the chamber.

El-Sayed's narrow primary victory over more moderate Rep. Haley Stevens in what was a divisive intraparty showdown was arguably the biggest victory to date for the left in its battle against the establishment for the ideological future of the Democratic Party. El-Sayed appeared this past weekend at the state party's nominating convention in Lansing, Michigan in an effort to unify Democrats in the wake of the primary battle.
DEMOCRATIC MICHIGAN AG ACCUSES HER PARTY OF 'ABSOLUTELY NOT' DOING ENOUGH TO COUNTER ANTISEMITISM
U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed speaks at the Michigan Democratic Party convention, on August 29, 2026, in Lansing, Michigan. (Peter D'Abrosca/Fox News Digital)

Fox News Digital asked El-Sayed about a recent controversy stemming from comments he made in response to an attack on a Michigan synagogue, when federal investigators say a gunman inspired and radicalized by Hezbollah crashed into the place of worship seeking to kill as many Jewish people as he could. The alleged attacker was a Lebanese-born man who a week earlier had lost relatives in an Israeli airstrike in Lebanon.

"Hurt people, hurt people," El-Sayed said in response to the attack. He was criticized by members of his own party, including Michigan Secretary of State Dana Nessel, who discussed the comments in a recent interview with The Atlantic, and declined to attend this past weekend's convention partly over concerns of antisemitism in the Democratic Party.
El-Sayed told Fox News Digital his comments "might have been misconstrued to be justifying something I did not intend to justify," but then offered an apology.

"To anybody who feels like my comments may have been hurtful, I’m really sorry. That was not my intention. We condemned that terrorist attack. We condemned it outright," El-Sayed added. "What I was trying to do was offer context for why it happened, but it wasn’t the time for context and you don’t ever want to trample somebody’s pain."

El-Sayed is an epidemiologist and former Wayne County Health Department director who, if elected in November, would make history as the nation's first Muslim senator. He has argued against unconditional U.S. military aid to Israel, as have other progressive politicians. And El-Sayed has repeatedly declined to directly answer whether Israel has the right to exist.

He said his message to Jewish voters in Michigan is, "We may not agree on everything when it comes to foreign policy... I'm not going to stop fighting for Palestinian self-determination... but that does not mean that I will not stand up… for safety for all communities and I believe in the safety and dignity of Jewish kids like I believe in the safety and dignity of my own kids."
Before taking questions from reporters, El-Sayed met in Lansing with the state's Democratic Jewish Caucus.
"He just had a very good meeting with us," Daniel Rivkin, a convention delegate and member of the caucus, told Fox News Digital, as he referred to El-Sayed. "We're having real conversations."
CHECK OUT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POLL IN MICHIGAN'S BLOCKBUSTER SENATE RACE

Former Rep. Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee in Michigan, announces support from Democrats as he launches a 'Dems for Mike' coalition, on August 20, 2026, in Detroit, Michigan. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
The El-Sayee campaign is also in the process of hiring a Jewish liaison, Fox News Digital confirmed on Monday.

But some Jewish leaders in Michigan went public on Saturday with an open letter urging Jewish Democrats and independents in the state to sign their names in support of Rogers, who is making a second straight run for the Senate after falling just 20,000 votes short in 2024.

"Many of us have been fiercely supportive of Democratic candidates and principles. All of us have felt threatened and alienated by the politics and allies embraced by Abdul El-Sayed, which has included demonization of Jews, equivocation on terrorism, exclusion of Jewish Americans from public life, and expression of implacable hatred of the world’s only Jewish nation," the letter stated.
Rogers, in a statement highlighting the letter, claimed that "Abdul El-Sayed fans the flames of antisemitism. We’re fighting to extinguish it."

In an interview Monday morning on Fox News' "Fox and Friends," Rogers said, "We've had so many Democrat Jewish people here in the state of Michigan ring up our phone and say, "I can't do this. I'm for you."
WHAT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS IN THE MIDTERM RACES SHOW
Referring to El-Sayed, Rogers said, "When someone says you might have been offended by what I said, that's not an apology."
And he claimed that El-Sayed "has a long history of antisemitic and inflammatory comments."

But El-Sayed has repeatedly pushed back, saying, "My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own kids. We have a responsibility to take on antisemitism in all of its forms, wherever we see it."
Making El-Sayed's mission to make peace with Jewish Democrats and independents more difficult is the backing he receives from Piker.

Piker recently featured on his stream an image of state Sen. Jeremy Moss, the Democratic nominee in Michigan's 11th Congressional District. Moss, who is Jewish, has said that people are sharing a fake audio clip of him claiming that his entire reason for running for Congress is to make sure that America continues to support Israel.

"If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action, not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews," Piker warned.
DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive candidate in the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate in Michigan, talks poolside with streamer Hasan Piker at a party for content creators supporting his campaign, Monday, Aug. 3, 2026, in Detroit. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)

Piker, who endorsed El-Sayed for the Democratic nomination and appeared at some of the candidate's campaign events including a primary night party in Detroit, has repeatedly stood by his numerous past comments critical of Israel over its ongoing war against Hamas in Gaza.

El-Sayed, who over the past week appeared to try and distance himself from Piker, responded to the firestorm by saying, "I want to be crystal clear, nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople."
On Saturday, El-Sayed was peppered with questions from reporters about Piker.

"We’re in the state of Michigan. If you want to make this race about a streamer in California, I just think you’re missing the boat," El-Sayed told reporters. "This is about affordability in Michigan. This is about seeing a doctor in Michigan. This is about Donald Trump’s disastrous policies in Michigan. That’s what I’m focused on right now."
As the questions about Piker continued, El-Sayed repeatedly characterized him as "a streamer from California" who is irrelevant to his race in Michigan. "This is not a serious conversation."
THESE 12 MIDTERM RACES WILL DECIDE WHICH PARTY CONTROLS THE SENATE
Besides his numerous antisemitic comments, Piker is known for saying "America deserved 9/11," praising Mao Zedong and Communist China, and arguing that capitalists should be murdered in the streets.

The Democrats' discord over Israel comes as most GOP leaders continue to showcase their support for Israeli leaders. As the Republican Jewish Coalition's annual leadership summit got underway Sunday evening in Las Vegas, El-Sayed and the far-left drew boos from the audience of high-powered GOP activists and donors.

Republican National Committee Chair Joe Gruters, speaking Monday at the RJC gathering, said that "the same hatred that fueled" the Oct. 7, 2023 large-scale attack by Hamas on Israel that killed about 1,200 people and triggered the ongoing war "is growing right here in our backyard."
"It has found a home in the Democratic Party. This did not happen overnight. It happened step-by-step as radical extremists took over the party, and the Democratic leaders let them," Gruters argued.
Meanwhile, there's no letup in the battle between the left and the center for the future of the Democratic Party.

Rahm Emanuel, a former ambassador, congressman, Chicago mayor and former White House chief of staff to then-President Barack Obama, took aim at the socialist push taking aim at the party's establishment.
"The Democratic Party is not open to being taken over," Emanuel, who's seriously mulling a 2028 White House run, told Fox News' Shannon Bream on "Fox News Sunday."
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"I don't consider the Democratic Socialists are part of the Democratic Party. About four weeks ago, they had a convention in Chicago. Separate party. They believe in defunding police, letting prisoners out of prison, opening borders, eliminating the Pentagon. If you're so confident people want that, I'll see you in November. Put it on the ballot. Let's go. Run as a separate party," Emanuel emphasized.
Democratic Party leaders, when asked about the party's current ideological warfare, often point to Democrats as a "big tent" party.
But veteran Democratic strategist Julian Epstein criticizes such responses and jabs at his party for failing to call out the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).

"They’ve taken cover behind the empty 'Big Tent" lie as radical DSA members and allies, like Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed and Colorado’s Melat Kiros, triumph in Democratic primaries," Epstein wrote in an opinion piece last week in the New York Post.

Epstein, who served as chief counsel for the Democratic minority on the House Judiciary Committee during the 1998 impeachment proceeds against then-President Bill Clinton and who later served on Hillary Clinton's presidential campaign, argued, "Moderates should unite and shed the Big Tent delusion — because they have nothing to lose but their chains."

With the House of Representatives back in session, a resolution "condemning socialism in all its forms" could see a vote later this week.

Rep. Jeff Crank, R-Colo., introduced a measure Thursday condemning socialism in all its forms, telling Fox News Digital he wanted to use the vote to force moderate House Democrats to take a more public stance against the DSA.
Fox News' James Cirrone contributed to this report
Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: New federal grand jury subpoena issued to former James Comey advisor in leak investigation: sources
summary: Former FBI Director James Comey faces a revived classified leak probe as a grand jury subpoenas his longtime adviser Daniel Richman on Monday.
story: Fox News' Chad Pergram reports the latest from Capitol Hill as Acting AG Todd Blanche is set to testify before lawmakers.

FIRST ON FOX: A federal grand jury issued a subpoena to former FBI Director James Comey's longtime friend and advisor on Monday as part of a new investigation into Comey allegedly leaking classified information to the media, multiple law enforcement sources told Fox News Digital.

The subpoena targets former Comey adviser Daniel Richman and indicates that the Justice Department has launched a fresh investigation into the leak of classified information to the New York Times. The issue was also investigated under President Donald Trump's first term, but was cut off when former President Joe Biden entered office.
The new investigation is in addition to the one centered on Comey's alleged threats against Trump.
TRUMP DOJ WITHDRAWS SUBPOENAS TARGETING NEW YORK TIMES JOURNALISTS AMID LEAK PROBE
Former FBI Director James Comey. (Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images)

Richman, a law professor and former attorney for Comey, played a central role in the initial investigation into the leak in 2018. He also later filed a lawsuit arguing that prosecutors violated his Fourth Amendment rights by seizing material from his electronic devices during investigations in 2019 and 2020.
A federal judge in Washington, D.C., ruled in his favor in that case in December of last year.
HEGSETH ANNOUNCES JOINT TASK FORCE WITH DOJ TO PROSECUTE LEAKS TO JOURNALISTS 'WITH THE FULL FORCE OF THE LAW'

Prosecutors had relied on the files to indict Comey on charges of making false statements and obstructing Congress in connection with his 2020 testimony on FBI officials anonymously giving information to news outlets.

The indictment accused Richman, previously a special FBI employee, of communicating with reporters about investigations into 2016 presidential candidate Hillary Clinton in that year's election loss to President Donald Trump.
COMEY LEARNS FATE OF BID TO DELAY TRIAL OVER ‘86 47’ SEASHELL POST AT CENTER OF TRUMP THREAT CASE

Daniel Richman, a professor at Columbia Law School in New York, testifies before the Senate Committee on the Judiciary on September 18, 2007, in Washington, D.C.  (Photo by Stephanie Kuykendal/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The new case comes as Comey is also facing litigation over his "86 47" Instagram post, which prosecutors argue constituted a threat against Trump.
Comey is facing two federal charges and up to 10 years in prison in that case, though the original prosecutor in the case resigned in early June.
BLANCHE TURNS THE TABLES ON COMEY INDICTMENT CRITICS: ‘REST ASSURED’ CASE GOES BEYOND INSTAGRAM POST

"Threatening the life of the President of the United States is a grave violation of our nation’s laws," acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said in an April 28 statement at the time the two-count indictment for threatening the president and transmitting a threat in interstate commerce was announced.
Former FBI Director James Comey's old notes are coming back to haunt him. (Jonathan Ernst/Reuters)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"The grand jury returned an indictment alleging James Comey did just that, at a time when this country has witnessed violent incitement followed by deadly actions against President Trump and other elected officials," he added. "The temperature needs to be turned down, and anyone who dials it up and threatens the life of the President will be held accountable."
Brooke Taylor is a Dallas-based correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). She joined the network in 2024.

title: FIRST ON FOX: Texas becomes testing ground for new defense against attacks on America’s water systems
summary: Project Watershed 250 pairs AI security tools with Texas water systems to find cyber vulnerabilities before adversaries can exploit them first.
story: Fox News chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin reports on the Trump administration’s program to protect U.S. water systems following alleged foreign hacking attempts on ‘Special Report.’

FIRST ON FOX: The Trump administration is launching "Project Watershed 250" Monday, Fox News Digital exclusively learned, deploying American artificial intelligence and cybersecurity tools to protect Texas water systems from cyberattacks in a pilot the administration plans to scale nationwide.

"Project Watershed 250 is another example of President Trump putting American families and communities first. President Trump is relentless in his work to secure our critical infrastructure against our most determined adversaries," National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross told Fox News Digital. "President Trump has cemented America’s leadership in AI security and innovation and is now bringing those exquisite tools to local communities and utilities in Texas and ultimately, across the nation through the launch of Project Watershed 250 – a scalable cyber water pilot program."

The Trump administration is bringing federal, state and private-sector cyber defenses together in a six-month Texas pilot aimed at finding vulnerabilities in water systems before adversaries can exploit them — while testing whether the model can be expanded across the country.
INVESTIGATORS BELIEVE IRANIAN HACKERS ARE LIKELY BEHIND CYBERATTACK ON MINNESOTA WATER SYSTEMS: REPORT
President Donald Trump speaks during an executive order signing in the Oval Office of the White House on June 22, 2026. (Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The program will connect Texas water utilities with U.S. cybersecurity companies to test their existing defenses and strengthen vulnerable systems using private-sector cyber and artificial intelligence tools, a White House official told Fox News Digital.

The program will use "red-teaming" to stress-test water utilities’ networks, identify weaknesses hackers could exploit and then strengthen those systems with cybersecurity tools, according to a White House official.
TRUMP LAUNCHES GOLD EAGLE TO HUNT CYBER FLAWS WITH AI

An official said the program is not in response to cyberattacks on Minnesota water systems, though the incidents underscored vulnerabilities in local infrastructure. (Thomas Trutschel/Photothek via Getty Images)

Dragos CEO Robert Lee said that U.S. water infrastructure faces active, documented threats, particularly at small utilities that often lack strong cybersecurity defenses. Lee said Watershed 250 will help get technology, training and support to those vulnerable systems before an attack occurs.

"There is nothing more important to Texans than clean, reliable drinking water. Project Watershed 250 puts federal, state, and private-sector cyber defenses behind our utilities at no cost. The White House, the Texas Cyber Command, and industry now work from the same playbook," said Texas Gov. Greg Abbott.

A White House official, however, said the program is not in response to recent cyberattacks that targeted more than 30 Minnesota water systems, though the incidents underscored vulnerabilities in local infrastructure.

"However, these recent attacks have reiterated the need for this modernization and focus on water systems," said the White House official. "Critical Infrastructure protection has long been a priority for ONCD and President Trump and this effort has been in the works since last year."
IRANIAN HACKERS ATTACKED OUR WATER SYSTEMS. HERE ARE 5 THINGS OUR LEADERS NEED TO DO NOW
President Donald Trump wraps up his speech at the opening of the Great American State Fair, June 24, 2026, on the National Mall in Washington. (Jacquelyn Martin/AP)

The Environmental Protection Agency and Department of Homeland Security’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency will serve as federal partners in the effort, while Texas Cyber Command will work alongside the White House with local governments and tech companies such as Microsoft, Reflection AI, Palo Alto Networks and Dragos Inc.

"Few things matter more than the safety of the water Americans drink, and this is a powerful example of how open-weight AI models, built in the U.S. and running on a utility’s own systems, can help keep communities safe," said Becky Sosnov, Reflection AI head of corporate affairs.
ANTHROPIC'S MYTHOS AI FOUND OVER 2,000 UNKNOWN SOFTWARE VULNERABILITIES IN JUST SEVEN WEEKS OF TESTING
A coordinated cyberattack reached operational technology at dozens of Minnesota water systems, exposing security risks for smaller utilities nationwide. (City of St. Cloud)
CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN

"Microsoft applauds the administration’s leadership in strengthening the cybersecurity of America’s water infrastructure and is proud to support the Project Watershed 250 effort in partnership with the Office of the National Cyber Director, the State of Texas, and Texas Cyber Command," said Microsoft US Public Sector president Chris Barry. "By bringing together Microsoft’s cybersecurity expertise, threat intelligence, and AI-powered security capabilities, we aim to help water utilities strengthen their resilience against evolving cyber threats and develop scalable approaches that can enhance the security of water systems nationwide."
The push comes as the Trump administration races to build out U.S. data centers to fuel the AI boom, putting more attention on the water and power needed to keep them running.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The pilot program builds on Trump’s June executive order on Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security and his Cyber Strategy for America released in March.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Vulnerable Dem's own audit admits Medicaid oversight failure amid massive statewide fraud scandal
summary: Matt Dunlap's office acknowledged a significant deficiency in tracking MaineCare payments as JD Vance calls Maine a fraud capital of America.
story: Maine whistleblower Christopher Bernardini alleges Minnesota-like fraud within the state's Medicaid program and explains its extent on ‘The Will Cain Show.’

Maine's Democratic state auditor, Matt Dunlap, who is now pursuing a bid to represent Maine's 2nd Congressional District, released a report earlier this year sounding the alarm that the state's internal watchdog for its MaineCare program had a serious gap in utilization control.

"[The Program Integrity Unit] could not provide documentation of the methodology used to identify projects and post-payment reviews performed in relation to surveillance of all Medicaid services provided under the State plan," the report reads, referring to the "PIU," the program's watchdog.

The report’s release, which comes after revelations of healthcare fraud in Maine from federal investigators and a local whistleblower, puts renewed focus on Dunlap’s tenure as auditor and raises questions about Maine's past systems to detect fraud amid one of the country's most competitive congressional races.
VANCE TURNS UP HEAT ON STATES WITH FEDERAL CASH THREAT OVER MEDICAID FRAUD CRACKDOWN
Maine state auditor Matt Dunlap, the Democratic congressional nominee in the state's 2nd District, is interviewed by Fox News Digital, on July 25, 2026, in Bangor, Maine. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

In order to ensure that state programs are complying with federal requirements, the PIU, the watchdog, selects a set number of cases for review, picking those cases based on "data analytics." The report didn't expand on those analytics — but noted a key weakness. In addition to being unable to provide documentation of why those cases had been chosen for review, the process also didn't take into account possible misuse — by patients or by the companies that bill MaineCare.

In the report's words, the PIU, the watchdog group, "does not document consideration of misutilization practices of beneficiaries or providers ... [and] may not provide adequate monitoring of all Medicaid services, resulting in potential noncompliance with Federal regulations."
Dunlap's 2026 report also acknowledged that this particular reporting issue hadn't been caught before, noting that it had a "prior year findings: none" designation.

When asked about the weakness and whether this was really the first time it had surfaced in an audit, Dunlap's campaign stressed that the report only narrowly applied to that particular weakness and that Dunlap had received praise — even from local Republicans — on his work identifying other liabilities.

"As Auditor, Matt Dunlap has flagged many issues that date back to the LePage administration. He has been praised by local press and Republican leaders alike for his work to recommend ways to safeguard taxpayer dollars. Paul LePage should answer why his team didn't implement the recommendations of his own Auditors from when he was governor," Harry Burke, a spokesperson for the Dunlap campaign said in a comment to Fox News Digital, referring to the Republican nominee in the race, a former governor of Maine who served from 2011 to 2019.

The campaign also observed that Dunlap himself, as an auditor, has little power to implement changes he flags as problematic. Decisions to remedy issues within Maine's programs lie within the departments themselves, although auditors can recommend specific changes.

"The auditor's job is to be a fire alarm: identify the problems so that state agencies can act. For example, last year, his recommendations led to the arrest and prosecution of a procurement fraudster saving taxpayer dollars," Burke added.
Despite his campaign's pushback, Dunlap has received backlash from Republicans for failing to stop fraud schemes that have caught national attention.
TRUMP TASK FORCE IS TACKLING $250 BILLION IN GOVERNMENT FRAUD. IT’S JUST GETTING STARTED

Vice President JD Vance spoke during a news conference on anti-fraud initiatives in the Indian Treaty Room of the Eisenhower Executive Office Building on May 13, 2026, in Washington, D.C. The Trump administration warned states they could lose Medicaid funding if they fail to comply with federal anti-fraud statutes. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Dunlap first came into the role in 2021 despite lacking the credentials to become an auditor. After being installed, he had to resign after twice failing the needed tests to become a certified auditor. Even so, Dunlap returned to the role in November 2022 after passing the requisite exams.

That track record has become a focal point for Republicans in the congressional race after the U.S. Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General revealed in January that the state had paid out at least $45.6 million in improper Medicaid payments for autism services.
The findings only furthered concerns raised by a whistleblower in December.

Christopher Bernardini, a former employee of Gateway Community Services, said his company had been defrauding Maine’s Medicaid program. According to Bernardini, the health services contractor had routinely filed false records about client visits, billing the state for services that Gateway had never provided.
The compounding stories of fraud have captured the attention of figures like Vice President JD Vance, who highlighted them in a visit to the state on Monday.
"How did Maine become one of the main capitals of defrauding the American taxpayer?’" Vance asked at a campaign event.

"One of the answers is somehow you guys hired an auditor who is not actually an auditor and failed the auditor exam. Well, call it old-fashioned common sense, but if you want somebody managing your money, maybe they ought to actually meet the constitutional requirements to do the job," Vance said.
Vance argued Dunlap’s track record should be disqualifying.

"And for Matt Dunlap, if you’ve got a guy who cannot protect your tax dollars from fraudsters, who has turned your state into one of the fraud capitals of the United States of America, maybe you should be saying to Matt Dunlap, ‘You’re fired, not promoted to the United States Congress,’" Vance said.
Previous years of reporting before Dunlap’s time as auditor also cast doubt on the office’s aggressiveness in uncovering fraud, hinting that the office’s zeal has declined under his watch.
Notably, in the six years before Dunlap took over the reins in 2022, the state had identified that it had almost too many active fraud investigations.
"Cases opened because of potential fraud, abuse, or questionable practices need improved supervisory review," several reports state.
Audits going back to 2016 noted that the office had routinely taken on more cases than its resources and its staffing would allow for, leading to a lack of monitoring of individual cases.
DR. OZ NAMES 5 STATES IN FRAUD CRACKDOWN AS TRUMP ADMIN TARGETS MEDICAID ABUSE
Maine state auditor Matt Dunlap is primary challenging Democratic Rep. Jared Golden in the state's Second Congressional District. (Matt Dunlap for Congress)
Since Dunlap returned to the role in 2022, the auditor’s office has not resurfaced that concern.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Having secured his party’s nomination in the state’s primaries earlier this year, Dunlap heads to the general election on Nov. 3, where he faces off against the Republican nominee, former Gov. Paul LePage.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: 'Jesus was a radical': Progressives invoke Christ to sell left-wing agenda on campaign trail
summary: Angie Nixon, Abdul El-Sayed and James Talarico are weaving faith into their Senate campaigns, drawing comparisons to Jesus and echoing the Moral Majority.
story: Florida Democratic Senate nominee Angie Nixon took a page from Abdul El-Sayed's book and compared her "radical" positions to Jesus in an unearthed clip. (Credit: St. Paul AME Jacksonville - Aug. 23)
Progressives seeking a seat in the Senate are taking a decades-old page from their Republican counterparts, using faith as a political tool to build connections with voters.

Three progressive Democratic candidates running for the Senate, Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon, Abdul El-Sayed and Texas state Rep. James Talarico, share a penchant for bucking the Democratic establishment in their meteoric rise this midterm cycle.

They have also incorporated their religions and faiths into their campaigns and messaging to voters, showing shades of the "Moral Majority" coalition that formed during the late 1970s in the GOP when former President Ronald Reagan was running as Republicans sought to tie policy to Christianity.
PROGRESSIVE FLORIDA LAWMAKER ANGIE NIXON TOPPLES TRUMP IMPEACHMENT WITNESS IN DEM SENATE PRIMARY UPSET

Progressive hopefuls are lifting a page from Republicans' playbook and tying faith to their policy platforms. (Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images; Jeff Kowalsky/AFP via Getty Images; Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

Nixon, who scored a major upset against Alexander Vindman, a major figure during President Donald Trump’s first impeachment trial who was backed by the Democratic establishment in Washington, D.C., has become a prime target for the GOP because of her connection to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).

During a sermon last week at the Saint Paul AME Church of Jacksonville, Fla., Nixon, who will face Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla., in November, contended that her "radical" positions were akin to those of Jesus Christ.
"They are trying, y'all. They are trying … to label me as this extremist, this radical. But, you know, Jesus was a radical," Nixon said.
EL-SAYED MAKES JESUS COMPARISON WHEN PRESSED ON SOCIALIST VIEWS: 'RADICAL IN HIS TIME, TOO'

"And Jesus fought for — I mean, he pushed for the same things that I'm fighting for today, right? Right now, we're literally in a civil rights moment," she continued. "Whether or not people wanna believe it or not, but we are."

She joined the DSA in June, prompting immediate backlash from the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC), the Senate GOP’s campaign arm, which tied her to socialism, despite her denial that she’s a Democratic socialist.
Nixon isn’t the only one of the three to make the same comparison.

El-Sayed, during an appearance on the Progressive Christians Podcast that aired in May, similarly invoked Christ when asked about his policy positions. El-Sayed, who is Muslim and running in Michigan’s toss-up race against former Rep. Mike Rogers, was asked about the similarities between his faith and Christianity and why they were being targeted as radical.
"Well, you know, Jesus, peace and blessings be upon him, was considered radical in his time, too," El-Sayed said.
JAMES TALARICO ADMITS PAST COMMENTS 'MISSED THE MARK' WHEN CONFRONTED ON CLAIMS LIKE GOD IS 'NON-BINARY'

"And there is a radical nature to being willing to stand forthright in a time of corruption, and I think it's important for all of us to realize that popularity and zeitgeist don't make truth. And we live in a time where people are trying to normalize corruption," he continued.

Of the three, Talarico, who is running in the toss-up race against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, has displayed his faith the most. He has been taking seminary classes to become a Presbyterian minister, and has blended Christianity with his policy platform since launching his candidacy last year.
And like the others, Republicans have pounced on his use of faith as a point of attack, particularly in his defense of transgender children.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
In pushing back against the Texas GOP’s newly signed anti-trans bill in 2021, Talarico argued Texas Republicans were trying to justify the measure "in the name of God's law."

"The first two lines of the Bible, the first two lines in Genesis, use two different Hebrew words to describe God. One is the masculine Hebrew noun for divinity," Talarico said. "The second is the feminine Hebrew noun for spirit. God is both masculine and feminine, and everything in between."
"God is non-binary," he said.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Newly unclassified Pentagon images show suspected drug boats as official issues deadly warning
summary: Exclusive Pentagon photos show suspected drug-smuggling boats under U.S. military surveillance as Operation Southern Spear reaches 67 strikes at sea.
story: SOUTHCOM carried carried out a lethal strike on a go-fast boat along a known trafficking route. Chief Gen. Francis L. Donovan says Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere will "hunt, disrupt, and defeat" cartel networks.
EXCLUSIVE – Newly unclassified Pentagon images show suspected drug-smuggling boats at sea, including vessels loaded with apparent narcotics.

The images come as the department warned traffickers that the U.S. will continue hunting down those who threaten Americans, nearly a year after the Trump administration began striking suspected drug-trafficking vessels.

"Nearly one year after the first strike, the message to narco-terrorists remains unchanged: if you traffic deadly illicit narcotics and threaten the American people, we hunt you down, we will find you, and we will kill you," Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital.
The photos, dated Oct. 27, Oct. 29 and Dec. 4, 2025, show the boats speeding through open water under U.S. military surveillance.
DEM SENATOR ACCUSES PENTAGON OF MURDER WITH BOAT STRIKES TARGETING DRUG TRAFFICKERS
An unclassified Pentagon image dated Oct. 27, 2025, shows a suspected drug-smuggling vessel carrying apparent narcotics at sea. (Department of War)
Wilson said Operation Southern Spear has disrupted trafficking networks, forced traffickers to adapt their methods and removed "dangerous narcoterrorists."
US MILITARY CONDUCTS MORE DEADLY STRIKES AGAINST VESSELS OF ALLEGED 'NARCO-TERRORISTS'
An unclassified Pentagon image dated Oct. 29, 2025, shows a suspected drug-smuggling boat at sea. (Department of War)

"Operation Southern Spear has disrupted trafficking networks, forced trafficker adaptations, removed dangerous narcoterrorists, and demonstrated that the United States will use every lawful tool available to defend our Homeland and protect our communities," Wilson said.
The Pentagon told Fox News Digital the operation has carried out 67 strikes, including the first strike on Sept. 2, 2025.
US KILLS TWO 'NARCO-TERRORISTS' IN STRIKE 2 MONTHS SINCE LAST ANNOUNCED ANTI-'NARCO-TRAFFICKING' ATTACK
An unclassified Pentagon image dated Dec. 4, 2025, shows a suspected drug-smuggling boat at sea. (Department of War)
One of the most recent strikes came Aug. 25, when U.S. Southern Command said four alleged drug smugglers were killed aboard a fast boat operating along known trafficking routes in the Caribbean.

"Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking," SOUTHCOM wrote in a post on X, saying the operation was carried out by Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere under the direction of Gen. Francis L. Donovan.
US MILITARY KILLS THREE 'NARCO-TERRORISTS' IN LATEST LETHAL STRIKE ON VESSEL IN THE EASTERN PACIFIC

"Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere continues executing precise, lethal operations against the cartels," Donovan said in a statement quoted in the post. "We will hunt, disrupt, and defeat these narco-terrorist networks."
"SOUTHCOM is resolved to neutralizing cartel terror and violence throughout the region and into the U.S. homeland," he added.
US MILITARY CONDUCTS STRIKE ON ANOTHER VESSEL CARRYING ALLEGED NARCO-TRAFFICKERS, KILLING 2

Days before the Caribbean strike, the U.S. military said two people were killed in a strike on a vessel in the Eastern Pacific. That was the first reported strike in more than two months. A video posted to X showed what appeared to be a moving boat before a flash filled the screen.
Since the first strike last September, the Trump administration has targeted suspected cartel vessels in the Atlantic and Pacific that it says were carrying narcotics.
PRESIDENT TRUMP’S DRUG CONTROL STRATEGY SETS THE PATH TO END THE DRUG CRISIS FOR GOOD

Trump has described the fight as an "armed conflict" with cartels in Latin America and has argued the attacks are necessary to stop drugs from reaching American communities and fueling fatal overdoses.
The administration is also pursuing agreements with allied nations that could extend its campaign onto land in multiple Latin American countries.

War Secretary Pete Hegseth said during a visit to Panama this month that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow the U.S. to conduct joint operations against criminal groups on their soil, though Guatemala denied an agreement had been reached. Ecuador began similar missions with the U.S. in March.
